entries.title: Slippage tolerance exceeded
entries.summary: The price moved further than the slippage you allowed, so the router refused to fill the trade and cancelled it. Nothing was swapped and no tokens moved.
why: Slippage is a maximum acceptable price drift. If the pool price is outside that band when the transaction lands, the program aborts on purpose.
Common in fast-moving or thin markets: new token launches, low-liquidity pools, or a busy block where your transaction sat for several seconds.
It is also the single most common error on Solana DEX aggregators, so seeing it does not mean your wallet or funds are broken.
fix: Raise the slippage limit slightly (for example 0.5% to 1% on liquid pairs) and retry - but never set a very high value on a thin token, that is how you get filled at a terrible price.
Reduce the trade size so the pool impact stays inside your tolerance.
Increase the priority fee so the transaction lands in the next block instead of waiting.
If it fails repeatedly on the same pair with high slippage, the pool liquidity is probably too thin - pick a different route or pool.

entries.title: Not enough token balance
entries.summary: The token account does not hold enough of the token to cover the transfer, or the amount was already spent by an earlier instruction in the same transaction.
why: The amount in the swap or transfer is larger than the balance, including the case where two instructions in one transaction compete for the same tokens.
The value you see in your wallet may include tokens that are still locked in an open order, or a balance the interface rounded up.
Token-2022 tokens can also carry a transfer fee, so the amount that arrives is smaller than the amount you sent.
fix: Refresh the wallet balance and retry with a slightly smaller amount - leave a little room for fees and rounding.
If you just moved these tokens in another tab, wait for that transaction to confirm first.
For Token-2022 mints, add the transfer fee to the amount you send.

entries.title: Not enough SOL to pay the fee
entries.summary: The fee payer did not have enough SOL to cover the network fee plus the rent for any new accounts the transaction creates.
why: Every transaction needs a small SOL balance in the fee payer's wallet - typically a fraction of a cent, but it must exist.
Creating a new token account costs about 0.00204 SOL of rent, which is easy to forget when you have just emptied a wallet.
Some wallets show a rounded 0.00 balance while a few thousand lamports are still technically present, which is not enough for a transaction.
fix: Send a small amount of SOL to the wallet and retry - 0.01 SOL covers hundreds of simple transactions.
If you are closing accounts to recover rent, do that first and use the recovered SOL for the next transaction.
Check that you are using the same wallet as the fee payer that the interface expects.
entries.example: Transaction simulation failed: Attempt to debit an account but found no record of a prior credit.

entries.title: Blockhash not found (expired)
entries.summary: The transaction referenced a recent blockhash that has already expired, so the network refuses to process it. This is a timeout, not a failure of your funds.
why: A Solana blockhash is valid for roughly 60 to 90 seconds. If the transaction is signed and then not submitted in time, it is rejected.
A wallet that is offline, a phone that locks, or a confirmation screen left open too long all cause this.
It also happens when the network is congested and the transaction is dropped before landing.
fix: Simply retry - your wallet will fetch a fresh blockhash and sign again.
Keep the confirmation screen in the foreground until the transaction is submitted.
Add a higher priority fee during busy periods so the transaction lands inside the blockhash window.
entries.example: Transaction simulation failed: Blockhash not found

entries.title: Token account is frozen
entries.summary: The token's issuer froze this token account, so it cannot send or receive that token until the issuer unfreezes it.
why: Mints created with a freeze authority allow the issuer to freeze individual token accounts - common for regulated stablecoins and some launchpads.
The freeze is applied to the account, not the wallet, so other tokens in the same wallet are unaffected.
Trying to swap or transfer the frozen token will always fail with this code until the issuer acts.
fix: Contact the token issuer - only the freeze authority can unfreeze the account.
Verify on a block explorer that the account really shows as frozen before assuming a wallet bug.
Do not pay anyone who claims they can unfreeze it for a fee; only the issuer's authority key can do this.

entries.title: Token account owner mismatch
entries.summary: The token account is owned by a different wallet than the one signing, so the program refuses to move the tokens.
why: You are trying to spend from a token account that belongs to another wallet - often after switching accounts in the wallet extension.
A delegated account was revoked, or the delegation expired.
The interface passed the wrong token account for this mint.
fix: Confirm the active wallet in your extension matches the one that owns the tokens.
Reconnect the wallet to the dApp so it re-reads the account list.
If you were using a delegate, ask the owner to re-approve it.

entries.title: Account not initialized or not found on chain
entries.summary: An account the transaction expects does not exist yet on chain, so the program cannot read or write it.
why: The associated token account for that mint was never created for this wallet.
The account was closed in an earlier transaction - for example by a rent-reclaim action.
A program-derived address is derived from inputs that do not match what the program expects.
fix: Create the associated token account first - most swap interfaces do this automatically, but a custom script may not.
Re-run the action from the official interface rather than a cached page.
If the account was closed on purpose, re-create it before transferring into it.

entries.title: Transaction already processed
entries.summary: This exact signed transaction was already submitted and processed. It is usually a duplicate submission, not a new failure.
why: You pressed the confirm button twice, or the wallet retried while the first submission was still in flight.
A relayer or bot re-sent the same signed bytes.
The transaction actually succeeded earlier - check the first submission before retrying.
fix: Look up the signature on an explorer to see whether the first attempt landed.
Do not resubmit: build a fresh transaction if you need to act again.
If your wallet keeps auto-retrying, wait a few seconds before pressing confirm again.
entries.example: Transaction simulation failed: This transaction has already been processed

entries.title: Compute budget exceeded
entries.summary: The transaction ran out of compute units before it finished, so the program was aborted mid-way.
why: Every transaction has a compute ceiling. Complex routes - many hops, many accounts, big token lists - can exceed the default.
A program looped longer than expected because of unusual pool state.
The priority fee was raised but the compute limit was left at the default.
fix: Raise the compute unit limit in the interface (advanced settings) and retry.
Split a large multi-hop swap into two smaller swaps.
Use a simpler route or a different aggregator for that pair.
entries.example: Program ... failed: Program failed to complete: exceeded maximum number of instructions allowed

entries.title: Custom program error (unknown code)
entries.summary: A program rejected the transaction with an error code that only its own developers define. The logs around the failure usually reveal the reason.
why: Each on-chain program defines its own error enum; code 6001 on one program can mean something completely different on another.
Newer programs and forks often reuse codes without publishing a mapping.
Most of these turn out to be slippage, a missing account, or a permission check.
fix: Read the last few log lines - programs usually print the human reason right before failing.
Retry once with a fresh blockhash and a slightly higher priority fee; transient state causes many of these.
If it repeats on the same action, open a support ticket with the signature - the program team can decode it instantly.

entries.title: Network too busy to include the transaction
entries.summary: The transaction was dropped because the block or the account was oversubscribed. Nothing happened on chain.
why: Hot mints and popular launches create contention on the same accounts, and the scheduler drops the excess.
The block cost limit was reached before your transaction could be included.
Priority fee was below what the current slot required.
fix: Retry with a higher priority fee.
Wait for the launch rush to pass if you are minting something popular.
Use a wallet or interface that supports Jito bundles or retry logic.

entries.title: Signature verification failed
entries.summary: The signature on the transaction did not match the message. The wallet signed different bytes than what was submitted.
why: The transaction was modified after signing - some wallets add a priority fee after the fact.
You are submitting a transaction built for a different cluster (devnet versus mainnet).
A hardware wallet signed an older version of the message.
fix: Sign again from the same wallet without editing fees in another tab.
Check the network selector - devnet transactions never work on mainnet.
Reconnect the hardware wallet and rebuild the transaction.
entries.example: Transaction simulation failed: Signature verification failed

entries.title: Malformed or unsupported transaction
entries.summary: The transaction could not be parsed by the node - it is structurally invalid or uses a version the endpoint does not support.
why: A custom script built the message with the wrong account ordering or a bad instruction layout.
The transaction is a versioned transaction being fetched without version support enabled.
A wallet produced bytes for a different runtime.
fix: Rebuild the transaction with an up-to-date SDK.
When reading versioned transactions, request maxSupportedTransactionVersion.
Use the official interface for that program instead of a hand-rolled script.
entries.example: Transaction simulation failed: Transaction did not pass sanitization

entries.title: Insufficient funds for rent (SOL)
entries.summary: Creating or funding an account would leave it below the rent-exempt minimum, so the network rejected the transaction.
why: Every account must hold a minimum SOL balance to stay alive; a partial funding amount is rejected outright.
Sending an amount that leaves an account between zero and the rent minimum is not allowed.
Closing an account and immediately spending the recovered rent can produce this error.
fix: Fund the account with at least the rent-exempt minimum (about 0.00089 SOL for a basic account, about 0.00204 SOL for a token account).
Top the wallet up with a small amount of SOL and retry.
If you are sweeping a wallet, keep enough SOL behind for rent.

entries.title: Account would not be rent exempt
entries.summary: The token account would end up below the rent-exempt threshold, which the token program refuses to allow.
why: You are withdrawing almost all SOL or tokens from an account that must keep a minimum balance.
The account was funded with an amount just under the threshold.
A close-account instruction was skipped before the withdrawal.
fix: Leave at least the rent-exempt minimum in the account.
Close the account properly instead of draining it.
Top up the account so it clears the threshold.

entries.title: Mint mismatch
entries.summary: The token account holds a different mint than the one the instruction expects - usually a stale or wrong account was passed in.
why: Two tokens share a similar symbol, and the interface passed the wrong mint address.
The cached account list is out of date after a swap or a burn.
A custom script reused an account variable for a different mint.
fix: Reload the page so the interface re-reads your token accounts.
Double-check the mint address rather than the ticker symbol - symbols are not unique.
In a script, derive the associated token account from the mint every time.

entries.title: Invalid account state
entries.summary: The account exists but is not in a state the program can act on - for example an uninitialized or already-closed token account.
why: The account was closed but the interface still holds a reference to it.
Two transactions raced: one closed the account while the other was still using it.
The program expects an initialized mint or account and got an empty one.
fix: Retry after refreshing balances - the interface will re-create the account.
Wait for any in-flight transaction to confirm before acting again.
Re-create the associated token account for that mint.

entries.title: Token math overflow
entries.summary: An arithmetic operation inside the token program overflowed - the amount is larger than the token's supply or decimals can represent.
why: The transfer amount exceeds the mint supply or the maximum value for the token's decimals.
A calculation produced a negative or absurdly large intermediate value.
A custom program passed an unchecked amount.
fix: Check the amount and the mint's decimals - a decimal mismatch multiplies the value by powers of ten.
Send a smaller amount to confirm the route works.
If you are the program author, use checked arithmetic.

entries.title: Invalid slippage value
entries.summary: The slippage parameter itself was rejected - it was zero, negative, or above the program's allowed maximum.
why: Some routers enforce a hard ceiling on slippage to protect users.
A UI bug sent 0 or a value above 100 percent.
The parameter was in the wrong unit (basis points versus percent).
fix: Set a sane value - 0.1% to 1% for liquid pairs, up to a few percent for thin ones.
Refresh the interface; a stale form can keep resubmitting the bad value.
If you are integrating, check whether the program expects bps or a percentage.

entries.title: Missing platform fee account
entries.summary: The route expected a platform fee account that was not supplied, so the swap was rejected before executing.
why: The integrator's fee account was not created or not passed in.
You are calling the aggregator directly without the account list the interface normally builds.
A white-label front end has a misconfigured fee wallet.
fix: Use the official interface for that aggregator.
Create the fee account first if you are integrating.
Remove the platform fee parameter if you do not need it.

entries.title: Invalid calculation in the route
entries.summary: The program's internal math rejected the route - usually a tiny amount, an extreme price impact, or a pool with almost no liquidity.
why: The swap amount was dust-sized and the output rounded to zero.
Price impact was so large the calculation overflowed a bound.
The pool state changed between quote and execution.
fix: Increase the trade size above dust, or use a different pair.
Re-quote and retry immediately so the route matches current pool state.
Raise slippage slightly if the pool is volatile.

entries.title: Invalid input or output index
entries.summary: The route referenced a token position that does not exist in the account list - a malformed route rather than a market problem.
why: The integrator built a route with an index out of range.
Token ordering changed between quote and swap construction.
A custom script hard-coded indexes that no longer match.
fix: Re-quote and rebuild the transaction instead of reusing a cached route.
Use the official SDK to construct the swap.
Report the case to the interface if it repeats on a simple swap.

entries.title: Empty route
entries.summary: The route plan handed to Jupiter contained no swap steps at all, so there was nothing to execute. This is almost always an integration bug, not something a normal swap on jup.ag can trigger.
why: The routePlan passed to the route instruction was empty — a route was never built, or it was dropped when the transaction was assembled.
You only see this from custom integrations, scripts or third-party front-ends built on Jupiter's API. On jup.ag itself the route is always built for you.
fix: Refresh the page or get a new quote — if a front-end shows this, it is broken; report it to that front-end, not to your wallet.
If you are a developer: re-fetch the quote and rebuild the swap transaction; do not reuse a cached route plan from a previous quote.
Check that the route instruction's arguments were not stripped when you re-serialized the transaction.

entries.title: Not enough percent to 100
entries.summary: The route plan splits your input amount across several pools by percentage, and the percentages did not add up to 100%. Again an integration-side construction error.
why: A split route (for example 60% pool A + 30% pool B) only fills 90% of the input; the program rejects the remainder instead of guessing what to do with it.
Normal jup.ag swaps never expose this — the API always builds percentage-complete routes.
fix: Re-quote and retry through the official interface if a third-party UI produced this error.
Developers: verify that every route step's inPercent values sum to exactly 100 (values are in hundredths of a percent — 10000 means 100%).

entries.title: Invalid token output index
entries.summary: The transaction referenced a token output index that does not exist in the route. An account-listing bug in whatever assembled the transaction.
why: Jupiter tracks intermediate tokens by index in the account list. An index pointing past the end of the list (or to the wrong account) is rejected before any swap executes.
Seen only in custom integrations or badly assembled transactions.
fix: Regenerate the swap transaction from a fresh quote instead of hand-editing account lists.
If you are integrating, confirm the destination token account was appended to the account array in the position the route plan expects.

entries.title: Not enough account keys
entries.summary: The transaction reached Jupiter missing accounts the route needs. Jupiter's own docs point to a modified swap transaction as the usual cause.
why: The swap transaction was edited after being built — accounts were removed, reordered, or an instruction was spliced in without adding its accounts.
Some wallets or front-ends try to shrink transactions to fit size limits and accidentally drop accounts the route still references.
fix: Use the swap transaction exactly as the API returned it — do not strip or reorder accounts.
Get a fresh quote; an expired route plan recombined with new accounts produces this error.
If your app needs to compress a transaction, use a smaller route instead of removing accounts.

entries.title: Non-zero minimum out amount not supported
entries.summary: A route step was built in a mode where a minimum output amount cannot be enforced, but a non-zero one was supplied. Integration construction error.
why: Certain swap modes (notably some shared-account and ledger-tracked routes) derive their limits internally and cannot honor an externally supplied minimum out amount.
You will not meet this on jup.ag; it appears in scripts that mix quote options incorrectly.
fix: Rebuild the transaction with minimumOutAmount = 0 for that route type, or pick a route mode that supports explicit minimums.
Developers: align your slippage handling with the mode you selected when requesting the quote.

entries.title: Invalid route plan
entries.summary: The route plan structure itself did not parse — steps out of order, wrong swap variant for the position, or a malformed split. Assembly bug territory.
why: Route plans are positional: each step encodes which swap variant runs and how it splits. A plan reordered or truncated no longer matches the transaction's account layout.
Usually caused by caching a stale quote and recombining it with new instructions.
fix: Discard the cached transaction, fetch a new quote, and rebuild from scratch.
Developers: serialize the routePlan field exactly as returned by the quote API.

entries.title: Invalid referral authority
entries.summary: A referral fee account was wired to an authority that does not match the referral program's records, so the fee leg of the swap was rejected.
why: Referral fees route a small share to a platform's fee account. The authority passed in must own that fee account.
Third-party front-ends that take a referral cut produce this when their fee account setup is broken or was rotated.
fix: Swap on jup.ag or another front-end that does not add a referral fee — nothing is wrong with your wallet.
If you run the front-end: re-derive the fee account PDA and confirm the authority matches your referral registration.

entries.title: Token ledger account mismatch
entries.summary: The route used a token ledger to track intermediate amounts, but the token account checked against it was not the one recorded. Routing assembly mismatch.
why: Split routes across the same pair use a token ledger to reconcile outputs between legs. Both legs must reference the same ledger and account.
This fires when one leg was rebuilt (new quote) while the other was not.
fix: Rebuild the whole transaction from a single fresh quote — mixing instructions from two quotes breaks the ledger pairing.
Developers: pass the same token ledger account to every leg of a split route.

entries.title: Invalid token ledger
entries.summary: The token ledger account passed to the swap is uninitialized, closed, or not a valid ledger. Integration bug.
why: Token ledgers are program-derived accounts created by a separate create_token_ledger instruction. If that instruction is missing or executed in the wrong order, the ledger is not there when the swap looks for it.
Only visible in custom integrations — jup.ag handles ledger creation for you.
fix: Re-quote and use the transaction as returned; do not drop the ledger setup instruction to save space.
Developers: ensure create_token_ledger runs before set_token_ledger, and set_token_ledger before the route instruction.

entries.title: Incorrect token program ID
entries.summary: A token program ID did not match the mint involved. Jupiter's docs call out platform fees on Token-2022 tokens as the classic trigger — the fee leg was wired to the legacy SPL Token program.
why: Solana has two token programs: the classic SPL Token program and Token-2022. A mint belongs to exactly one of them, and every account instruction must target the right one.
Front-ends that attach platform fees historically hardcoded the legacy program, so swaps involving Token-2022 mints failed on the fee leg.
Jupiter's troubleshooting page lists this exact scenario for 6014.
fix: Retry on jup.ag — the official interface resolves the correct token program per mint.
If it persists for one specific token, the token is likely Token-2022 and that front-end's fee path does not support it yet; swap without the referral fee or use another route.
Developers: resolve the token program from the mint's owner field instead of hardcoding Tokenkeg….

entries.title: Token program not provided
entries.summary: The route expected a token program account in the transaction and did not get one. Integration assembly bug.
why: Routes that can involve Token-2022 mints carry an explicit token program reference. Omitting it (for example, dropping an account to shorten the transaction) fails before execution.
Companion error to 6014 — that one is the wrong program, this one is no program.
fix: Use the unmodified transaction from the quote response.
Developers: include the token program account exactly where the route plan places it.

entries.title: Swap not supported
entries.summary: The requested swap shape is not one Jupiter's program can execute — typically an exotic route leg or an unsupported market type reached the program.
why: The quote API normally filters these out before building a transaction, so hitting 6016 means the transaction was assembled from a route the program cannot run.
Stale SDK versions can produce route plans newer routes no longer accept.
fix: Refresh and re-quote on jup.ag; the router will pick a supported route.
Developers: update the Jupiter SDK/API client — old cached route plans fail here after router upgrades.

entries.title: Exact-out amount not matched
entries.summary: An exact-out swap did not receive the required output amount. Jupiter's docs describe it as similar to slippage: the market moved and the fixed target could not be met.
why: Exact-out mode promises a specific amount of the destination token. If pools shifted between quote and execution, delivering that exact amount costs more than the program allows.
More sensitive than normal slippage because a single number must be hit exactly, not just bounded.
fix: Re-quote — in fast markets an exact-out quote is stale within seconds.
Use exact-in mode with a slippage limit instead; it tolerates movement far better.
Increase priority fee so the transaction lands closer to the block the quote was computed against.

entries.title: Source and destination mint are the same
entries.summary: The swap's input and output mint are the same token, which the router refuses — it would just shuffle tokens through pools and collect fees.
why: Usually a front-end bug: the destination token defaulted to the same mint as the input, or a wrap/unwrap was wired through the router instead of the token program.
Circular arbitrage (token → token) is explicitly disabled in the router.
fix: Pick a different destination token — if you really want to convert wrapped SOL to native SOL, use the wallet's unwrap action, not a Jupiter swap.
If a UI shows this for a normal-looking pair, it is a UI bug; reload and re-select the tokens.

entries.title: Invalid mint account
entries.summary: A mint account passed to the swap does not exist or is not a valid mint. Usually a fake, renamed, or extremely new token whose mint account was not what the route expected.
why: The mint address in the route must point to an initialized mint account. Scam tokens sometimes swap their mint or list a mint that is instantly closed.
Can also appear when a route was quoted for one mint and the transaction was built with another.
fix: Re-quote from the official interface — if the token is real, the router rebuilds the route with the correct mint.
Double-check the token you are trading: a mint mismatch during a token launch is a common sign of a copycat or scam listing.
Developers: verify the mint account exists and is owned by a token program before building the swap.

entries.title: Invalid program authority
entries.summary: An authority check on a Jupiter-owned account failed. You cannot cause this as a normal swapper — it points to a front-end or integration wiring the wrong PDA.
why: Jupiter derives program authorities (for shared accounts and open orders) as PDAs. A transaction that hardcodes or guesses these addresses fails the authority check.
Seen in hand-assembled transactions or SDK misuse.
fix: Use the transaction from the quote API unmodified.
Developers: derive PDAs with the official seeds rather than storing addresses.

entries.title: Invalid output token account
entries.summary: The destination token account handed to the swap is uninitialized, of the wrong mint, or otherwise not usable to receive the output. Jupiter's docs describe it as "a token account passed in is invalid".
why: The receiving account for the destination token either does not exist yet, belongs to the wrong mint, or is frozen.
Common right after buying a brand-new token: the wallet has not created that token account yet, and the front-end passed a placeholder.
Also fires when the ATA derivation was done for the wrong mint (copy-paste errors in integrations).
fix: Let the wallet create the destination token account first (opening the token's page in the wallet usually triggers it), then retry the swap.
Confirm you are not confusing the token's mint address with your token account address — the swap needs your account, not the mint.
Developers: pass an ATA derived for (owner, destination mint) and create it with the Associated Token Account program in the same transaction if needed.

entries.title: Invalid fee wallet
entries.summary: The platform fee wallet configured by the front-end is not a valid account. Front-end configuration problem, not your wallet.
why: Front-ends that charge a swap fee register a fee wallet. If that wallet account was closed, changed, or misconfigured, the fee leg fails.
You meet this only when swapping through a third-party interface with broken fee configuration.
fix: Swap on jup.ag directly — the official interface has valid fee configuration.
Report the error to the front-end; nothing in your wallet needs to change.

entries.title: Invalid authority
entries.summary: A signing authority in the transaction did not match what the program expected for one of the accounts involved.
why: Every token account operation must be signed by the account's owner or delegated authority. A transaction that lists the wrong signer — for example a program-derived address where a user key is required — fails here.
Typically an integration bug after authority handling changed.
fix: Retry the swap from the official interface; your own authority is always handled correctly there.
Developers: check that every account requiring your signature has you as a signer, and that delegated allowances match the delegate you actually signed with.

entries.title: Swap short of input funds
entries.summary: Jupiter's own funds check failed: not enough of the input token for the swap amount, or not enough SOL for fees and rent. Jupiter's docs list exactly those two buckets.
why: The input token balance is below the amount being swapped — including decimals rounding if you typed a max amount that the UI rounded up.
Or the fee payer cannot cover the network fee plus rent for accounts created during the route (intermediate token accounts are often opened and closed mid-route).
Note the difference from the SPL Token 0x1 error: 6024 is raised by Jupiter before its token transfers, with a clearer message about which bucket is short.
fix: Check the input token balance and swap slightly less than the maximum — UI "max" buttons are notorious for exceeding the real balance after decimals rounding.
Top up ~0.01-0.02 SOL in the fee payer wallet so fees plus rent are covered.
If the input balance looks right, check for a freeze or transfer hook on the token (Token-2022 extensions can block transfers) — the token page will show it.

entries.title: Invalid token account
entries.summary: One of the token accounts passed into the swap is invalid — uninitialized, wrong mint, or not the account the quote expected. Jupiter's docs: "A token account passed in is invalid, it can be uninitialized or not expected".
why: The front-end built the transaction against a token account that has since been closed, or never existed for that mint.
Happens frequently with brand-new tokens right after launch, when the account list changed between quote and execution.
Also fires when a UI confuses mint addresses with token account addresses.
fix: Re-quote and retry — a fresh quote rebuilds the account list against the current on-chain state.
Open the token in your wallet so the token account exists, then swap.
Developers: use the ATA program to create missing accounts inside the same transaction instead of assuming they exist.

entries.title: Bonding curve already completed
entries.summary: The route tried to buy from a Pump.fun-style bonding curve that has already graduated — the curve completed, migrated its liquidity to a DEX, and no longer sells from the curve.
why: Pump.fun tokens launch on a bonding curve. When the curve fills, it "graduates": the remaining liquidity moves to a standard AMM pool and the curve stops trading.
If your route was quoted while the token was still on its curve and executed after graduation, the curve leg fails with this error.
The name comes from Jupiter reusing this check for curve-type AMMs it routes to.
fix: Re-quote — the router will now route through the graduated token's AMM pool instead of the curve.
If the token just graduated, wait a few seconds; front-ends sometimes cache the old route aggressively.
You lost nothing but the fee: the transaction rolled back atomically.

entries.title: Invalid mint account
entries.summary: The mint account passed to a token instruction does not exist or is not a valid mint, so the token program rejected the instruction before anything moved.
why: Every token operation pairs accounts with a mint. If the mint address was typoed, renamed, or the token's mint was closed after creation, the pairing check fails.
Common around token launches where copycat contracts circulate several mint addresses that look identical.
Also fires when a mint address is pasted where a token account address is expected — the two look similar in base58.
fix: Verify the mint address against the token's official page (project site, CoinGecko, or the issuer's announcement) — not against what a random link told you.
Refresh the page and re-run the transaction; a just-created mint sometimes reaches wallets before their cache updates.
Developers: fetch the account and confirm its owner is a token program before using it as a mint.

entries.title: Fixed supply — cannot mint more
entries.summary: Someone tried to mint new tokens from a mint whose supply is fixed, and the token program refused.
why: A mint created without mint authority (or with authority renounced) can never mint again — this is by design for tokens that want a hard supply cap.
You see it when a mint instruction targets such a token: either the token's team attempted a mint that should not happen, or your app wired the wrong mint.
fix: Nothing to fix on your side as a holder — the supply is simply capped, as advertised.
If your own app hit this, remove the mint instruction or confirm the mint authority still exists before trying.
Be suspicious of a token whose docs promise future minting but whose mint authority is renounced.

entries.title: Token account already initialized
entries.summary: An initialize instruction targeted a token account that is already initialized, so the program refused to overwrite it.
why: Initializing an account twice would erase its state, so the program blocks it.
Almost always a double-submit: the create-account instruction ran once already (perhaps the earlier transaction landed), and a retry sends it again.
The good news: this error means the account you wanted exists — the goal is already achieved.
fix: Check the token account — it is most likely already created and usable; just run the transfer or swap you actually wanted.
Do not blindly retry the same transaction; if it was part of a bigger flow, re-run only the remaining steps.
Developers: skip initialize if the account is already initialized, or use idempotent ATA creation which tolerates this case.

entries.title: Invalid number of provided signers
entries.summary: The instruction required more (or fewer) signatures than the transaction actually carried. A transaction-assembly problem.
why: Multi-signature token operations (set authority on a multisig, transfer from a multisig account) declare how many signers must appear, and the mismatch fails immediately.
Single-owner wallets should never see this — when they do, the transaction was assembled with the wrong signer flags.
fix: Retry from the official interface — hand-built transactions usually carry the wrong signer count.
Developers: the signers parameter of the instruction must list accounts in the exact positions the instruction expects.

entries.title: Invalid number of required signers
entries.summary: The token account's declared required-signer count does not match what the instruction provided. The multisig counterpart of 0x7.
why: The account itself records how many signatures its operations need (m of n). The incoming transaction did not satisfy that record.
Appears when a multisig member count or threshold changed after the transaction was drafted.
fix: Rebuild the transaction with the current signer set for the multisig account.
Confirm the account's authority configuration — if the multisig was rotated, your transaction was drafted against the old state.

entries.title: Uninitialized account state
entries.summary: An operation hit a token account or mint that was never initialized, so there was no state to act on.
why: The account exists on chain but its initialize instruction never ran — often because the transaction that was supposed to initialize it failed earlier in the same atomic bundle.
Reading balances or transferring from an uninitialized account is impossible, so the program rejects early.
With Associated Token Accounts this is rare — the ATA program initializes on creation — but hand-created token accounts skip that step.
fix: Create/initialize the token account first (or let the swap or transfer instruction create it in the same transaction), then retry.
In a wallet, simply opening the token's page usually triggers account creation.
Developers: prepend a create-account instruction for any account your flow assumes exists.

entries.title: Instruction does not support native SOL
entries.summary: A token instruction that cannot apply to the special native-SOL account was sent against it.
why: Native SOL inside the token program lives in one shared special account; most operations (mint, freeze, set authority on it as if it were a normal mint) make no sense there.
Typically a bug in an app that treats wrapped SOL like any other token for administrative instructions.
fix: If you meant to wrap or unwrap SOL, use the wallet's dedicated wrap/unwrap action instead of a generic token instruction.
If you meant to move SOL, send it with a normal System Program transfer — no token instruction needed.

entries.title: Account not empty — cannot close
entries.summary: A close-account instruction ran on a token account that still holds tokens, which the program refuses so nothing is burned by accident.
why: Only accounts with exactly zero tokens can be closed. Dust amounts (a few decimal places left over after a swap) keep the account open.
Users often see this when sweeping wallets or cleaning up small positions.
fix: Transfer the remaining dust out (even to a burn address the token supports), or swap it, then close the account.
If the leftover is worthless, just leave the account open — it costs nothing once rent-exempt, and closing is optional.
Developers: pair close-account with a preceding transfer-all instruction in the same transaction.

entries.title: Invalid token instruction data
entries.summary: The instruction data sent to the token program could not be parsed — unknown instruction tag or malformed arguments.
why: The byte layout of the instruction did not match any known token instruction, usually from serialization bugs or a legacy instruction packed for a newer program (or vice versa).
Third-party front-ends that build their own token instructions occasionally emit the wrong packing.
fix: Retry through a maintained wallet or interface — their serialization is current.
Developers: regenerate instruction data with the current @solana/spl-token library instead of hand-packing buffers.

entries.title: Authority type not supported
entries.summary: A set-authority instruction asked for an authority type this account does not carry — the account has no such role to grant or revoke.
why: Token accounts carry freeze authority only via their mint, and mints carry mint/freeze authority. Requesting an authority type that does not exist on that account fails.
Often a mismatch: setting freeze authority on an account instead of the mint, or on a mint that never had one.
fix: Target the mint account for mint/freeze authority changes, not a token account.
Check the current authority layout on an explorer before retrying — you cannot set an authority type the program does not define for that account.

entries.title: This mint cannot freeze accounts
entries.summary: A freeze or thaw instruction was sent for a mint that has no freeze authority, so freezing is permanently impossible for that token.
why: A mint becomes freezable only if it was created with a freeze authority. Without one, no account of that token can ever be frozen — and freeze instructions are rejected.
For holders this is actually reassuring: the issuer cannot freeze your balance. The error usually means an app wrongly assumed the token is freezable.
fix: Nothing to do as a holder — skip the freeze-related step.
Apps: check whether the mint has a freeze authority before including freeze or thaw instructions in a transaction.

entries.title: Decimals mismatch
entries.summary: A decimals value supplied to the instruction does not match the mint's actual decimals, so the program rejected it rather than guessing.
why: Initializing a wrapped-SOL or new token account with a hardcoded decimals value that differs from the mint's real one.
Common with UIs that assume 9 decimals when the token uses 6 (USDT-style) or vice versa — amounts then display wildly wrong.
fix: Read the decimals from the mint account instead of hardcoding — the wallet displays the correct value on the token page.
If amounts in your app show absurd magnitudes (1000× off), this mismatch is almost certainly why.

entries.title: Instruction does not support non-native tokens
entries.summary: An instruction reserved for the native-SOL account was sent to a regular token account, where it has no meaning.
why: Only the special native-SOL account supports certain close/reclaim operations. Sending the same instruction against a normal token account fails.
Mirror error of 0xa — that one was a native-only instruction against a non-native account, this is the reverse.
fix: For regular tokens, use the standard close-account instruction to reclaim rent.
Developers: branch on whether the mint is the native SOL mint before choosing the close path.

entries.title: Not approved
entries.summary: The account signing the instruction is not the configured authority for this admin-only action. A normal swap or liquidity add never hits this — it is an operator or integration mistake.
why: Raydium CPMM keeps an AmmConfig account with an admin authority. Only that key can change fees, pause the pool, or update config.
Integrations that replay an admin instruction with a user's keypair, or with a stale config account, trigger it.
If you are a user and see this, the front-end is sending the wrong instruction type — nothing is wrong with your wallet or funds.
fix: Users: reload the front-end and retry the normal swap flow; do not sign an instruction labelled as a config change.
Integrators: verify the AmmConfig PDA you pass is the canonical one for the program, and that the signer is the configured admin.
If you are forking Raydium's admin tooling, check the authority keypair actually matches the on-chain config before sending.

entries.title: Input account owner is not the program address
entries.summary: An account passed into the instruction is owned by the wrong program — usually a wrong token program (SPL Token vs Token-2022) or a PDA from a different program entirely.
why: Every account in a Solana instruction declares an owner. CPMM checks that the pool, vault and mint accounts belong to the programs it expects.
Passing a Token-2022 account where the pool was created for SPL Token (or the reverse) is the classic cause.
It also fires when a client reuses a cached account list after the pool was recreated, so the PDAs no longer match.
fix: Refresh the pool data (re-fetch from api-v3.raydium.io) and rebuild the transaction instead of reusing cached accounts.
Check the mint's token program: a Token-2022 mint needs the Token-2022 program ID in the account list, not Tokenkeg.
If you are integrating, derive vault and pool PDAs from the program ID at runtime — never hardcode a pool's account set.

entries.title: Input token account empty
entries.summary: The LP token account or a pool vault had a zero balance at a step that requires a positive amount. Typically a withdraw or collect call with nothing to withdraw.
why: Withdrawing liquidity from a position that was already closed leaves the LP account at zero, but the instruction still demands a non-zero amount.
Collecting fees twice in a row produces the same result: the second call has nothing left to move.
It also appears if you add liquidity with an initial deposit of zero.
fix: Refresh the position and check the LP balance before withdrawing — a zero balance means the position is already closed.
Do not re-run a fee-collection call that just succeeded; the pool genuinely has nothing more to pay.
When adding liquidity, deposit a non-zero amount on both sides of the pair.

entries.title: InvalidInput
entries.summary: A generic argument rejection: an amount outside the allowed range, a flag that is not recognized, or a parameter combination the pool refuses.
why: CPMM validates argument ranges before doing math — a zero or absurdly large amount is rejected here rather than overflowing later.
Passing an amount with the wrong decimals (for example raw lamports where UI units were expected) lands in this branch.
Some instruction variants accept an option flag; an unexpected value fails this check.
fix: Check decimals: multiply UI amounts by 10^decimals before sending — a 6-decimal token needs 1,000,000 for one whole token.
Confirm the amount is strictly positive and below the pool's uint64 ceiling.
If you build instructions yourself, compare your argument layout against the current IDL — an added field silently shifts every later argument.

entries.title: Address of the provided LP token mint is incorrect
entries.summary: The LP mint account you passed does not match pool_state.lp_mint. Almost always a stale account list, or the LP mint of a different pool in the same pair.
why: Each CPMM pool has exactly one LP mint, recorded in pool state at initialization. The program rejects any other mint.
A pair can have several pools (different fee tiers or versions). Copying an LP mint from one into a call for another produces this error.
Cached front-end state after a pool migration can point at the old LP mint.
fix: Re-fetch the pool by its pool ID and read lp_mint directly from that pool's state — do not reuse an LP mint from a previous session.
If you hold LP tokens, check the mint on your token account in an explorer; it tells you which pool the position actually belongs to.
Rebuild the transaction from fresh pool data rather than patching the account list.

entries.title: Exceeds desired slippage limit
entries.summary: The executed price was worse than your minAmountOut / maxAmountIn, so the pool refused the trade. Identical in spirit to the Jupiter 6001 slippage error, but a completely different code namespace.
why: Every CPMM swap carries a slippage bound. If the pool's price moved outside it between quote and execution, the program aborts instead of filling at a bad price.
Thin pools and fast markets move several percent within a single block; a 0.1% limit on a new token will fail routinely.
It is also what you see when a front-end sends a stale quote with a hardcoded minimum out.
fix: Raise the slippage tolerance modestly (0.5–1% on liquid pairs, more only if you accept the price risk) and retry.
Cut the trade size so your own price impact stays inside the limit.
Add a priority fee so the transaction lands in the next block rather than aging while the price drifts.

entries.title: Given pool token amount results in zero trading tokens
entries.summary: The deposit or withdraw math rounded one side down to zero, because the amount was below the pool's minimum unit.
why: CPMM computes both sides of a liquidity operation from the LP amount. A dust-sized amount rounds to zero tokens on one side.
Tokens with few decimals (0 or 2) hit this quickly — one base unit is already a large fraction of a small deposit.
It also fires when withdrawing a near-zero LP balance left over from a previous partial exit.
fix: Increase the deposit or withdraw amount above the pool minimum; check the pool's decimals before choosing a number.
For a dust LP balance, withdraw the entire remaining position rather than a fraction of it.
If you only want to clear a position, use the close-position flow that handles dust explicitly.

entries.title: Not support token_2022 mint extension
entries.summary: The token is a Token-2022 mint using an extension CPMM cannot handle safely — most often TransferHook, or DefaultAccountState set to Frozen.
why: Token-2022 lets issuers attach behaviour to transfers: hooks that call another program, permanent delegates, transfer fees, frozen-by-default accounts.
CPMM supports only a subset. A hook or a default-frozen state has to be rejected, because the pool cannot guarantee the swap math holds.
It is a property of the token, not of your wallet or your amount — retrying will fail identically.
fix: Accept that this token cannot be traded through this CPMM pool; look for a venue that explicitly supports its extensions.
If you are the issuer, remove the unsupported extension (or launch the token without it) before seeking a CPMM pool.
Check the mint's extensions in an explorer under the Token Extensions tab to see exactly which one blocked you.

entries.title: Invalid vault
entries.summary: The vault account passed in does not match the one recorded in pool_state. Same family as the LP-mint error: a stale or foreign account list.
why: A CPMM pool records both token vaults at initialization. Only those two PDAs may be used for swaps and liquidity changes.
Passing a personal token account, or a vault belonging to a different pool of the same pair, fails this check.
After a pool is recreated (for example post-migration), clients holding the old vault addresses hit this every time.
fix: Re-derive the vault PDAs from the pool ID and the CPMM program ID, or read them from fresh pool state.
Never substitute your own ATA for a pool vault — the program moves funds only from its recorded vaults.
If you cached pool accounts, invalidate the cache whenever the pool's account data version changes.

entries.title: Init lp amount is too less
entries.summary: At pool creation the computed LP supply was below the permanently locked amount, so the pool would have been born with no tradable LP.
why: CPMM locks a fixed amount of LP at initialization to prevent a fully-drainable pool. Your initial deposit must exceed that floor.
Creating a pool with tiny amounts on one side produces a supply below the lock and is rejected.
It only appears at initialization — never on swaps or on later deposits.
fix: Increase the initial deposit on both sides; the pool needs enough total value to clear the permanent LP lock.
Match the ratio you intend to trade at, rather than depositing an arbitrary minimum.
If you only need a test pool, use devnet where the lock amount is not economically meaningful.

entries.title: TransferFee calculate not match
entries.summary: For a Token-2022 mint with a transfer fee, the observed post-transfer amount did not equal the pre-computed expectation — usually because the fee configuration changed mid-flight.
why: CPMM pre-computes the amount that will arrive after the token's transfer fee, then verifies it. A mismatch is treated as an unsafe state.
The issuer can change the fee via the TransferFeeConfig authority. If that happens between quote and execution, the numbers diverge.
Withholding-tax style extensions that accrue over time produce the same drift.
fix: Retry — a fresh quote after the fee change will compute correctly.
If it repeats on the same token, the issuer is actively changing fees; wait or use a venue that quotes the fee at execution time.
Integrators should read the current TransferFeeConfig immediately before building, not at page load.

entries.title: Math overflow
entries.summary: An intermediate swap, deposit or fee calculation exceeded the integer range the pool works in. In practice this means the amount was absurdly large for the pool.
why: CPMM keeps reserves in uint64/uint128 intermediates. A trade that would multiply beyond the ceiling is rejected instead of wrapping.
Depositing an amount with the wrong decimals (raw units where whole tokens were meant) produces exactly this.
Very imbalanced pools with extreme reserve ratios can overflow at smaller absolute sizes.
fix: Verify decimals — a 9-decimal token needs 10^9 per whole unit, so an extra three zeros can overflow a pool instantly.
Reduce the trade to a size the pool can absorb; check reserves before sizing.
Split a very large order across blocks rather than sending it as one swap.

entries.title: Insufficient vault
entries.summary: The pool vault does not hold enough of the output token to cover this trade. The pool's real liquidity is smaller than the quote implied.
why: Quotes are computed from reserves at quote time. If a large trade or a liquidity removal lands first, the vault can no longer pay out.
It is the on-chain version of 'price impact was underestimated' — the pool is genuinely short.
On a freshly created pool with asymmetric deposits, one side can be thin enough that modest trades exhaust it.
fix: Re-quote and reduce the size; the pool will tell you what it can actually fill now.
Pick a deeper pool for the same pair rather than pushing this one.
If you are the LP, note that removing most of one side is what causes this for traders.

entries.title: Invalid fee model
entries.summary: An admin tried to set an AmmConfig parameter combination the program rejects. Admin-only path — a normal user cannot trigger it.
why: Fee parameters have invariants: protocol fee plus fund fee plus creator fee must stay within bounds, and each must be below its ceiling.
The 2026-09 upgrade added fee-split fields; older tooling that omits them can compose an invalid model.
It appears only in config-change transactions, never in swaps.
fix: Admin: check every fee component against the current ceiling before submitting a config change.
Update admin tooling to the current IDL — added fee fields are the usual culprit after an upgrade.
Users who somehow see this: you are signing an admin instruction, which no legitimate trade flow asks for.

entries.title: Fee is zero
entries.summary: A fee-collection instruction found nothing collectable. On the permissionless creator-fee path this usually means both creator counters are still zero.
why: Fee counters accrue from trading volume. A pool with no swaps since the last collection has nothing to pay out.
Running collect twice in the same block gives the second call a zero balance and this error.
Creator fees may also be zero when the creator has already withdrawn everything.
fix: Treat it as a benign race rather than an error — there is nothing to collect, and nothing was lost.
Wait for trading volume before collecting again; repeated calls in the same block will keep failing.
Check the pool's fee counters on-chain to see when collection becomes worthwhile.

entries.title: Lamports calculate error
entries.summary: A wrapped-SOL round trip (sync native, unwrap) did not leave the wSOL balance exactly where it started. Added by the 2026-09 program upgrade.
why: CollectExcessLamports sweeps a wSOL account: it syncs the native balance, unwraps, then verifies the token balance is unchanged.
If lamports moved concurrently — another instruction touching the same wSOL account — the invariant fails.
It is an admin/maintenance path, not part of a normal swap.
fix: Retry when the account is not being modified by other instructions in the same transaction.
Do not bundle a wSOL balance sweep with a swap that also uses the same wSOL account.
Integrators: make sure wrapped SOL setup and unwrap happen in separate transactions.

entries.title: Not authorized
entries.summary: The account is not permitted to run this instruction — typically a creator-only action signed by someone else, or a PDA check that failed.
why: Pump.fun checks specific authorization relationships: the creator of a coin, the global authority, or a PDA signing derived from the curve.
Passing a different wallet as creator, or a curve account for a different mint, fails this check.
Bundler and auto-trading scripts often hit it when they reuse an instruction built for another wallet.
fix: Sign with the wallet that created the coin; creator-only actions cannot be delegated.
Re-derive the bonding curve PDA from the mint address rather than copying an address from another token.
If a third-party bot produced the transaction, it is building it for the wrong account — do not sign it.

entries.title: The program is already initialized
entries.summary: An initialize instruction ran against a store that already exists. Almost always a duplicate submission of a create/migrate call.
why: Global configuration and per-mint curve accounts are one-time initializations. Running them twice is a hard error.
Double-clicking a launch button, or a bot retrying without checking success, produces exactly this.
It also appears when a client races two transactions that both try to initialize the same account.
fix: Check whether the first transaction already confirmed before retrying — this error almost always means it did.
Do not re-submit a launch; the coin already exists at its mint address.
Clients should treat this as idempotent success rather than a failure to retry.

entries.title: Too much SOL required to buy
entries.summary: Buy-side slippage: filling your order would cost more SOL than your max SOL input allowed. The price moved up between quote and execution.
why: A buy on the curve takes SOL in and returns tokens. Your limit is expressed as a maximum SOL cost; if the curve moved up, the cost exceeds it.
Bonding curves are steep near the top — a coin in its last stretch can move several percent per slot.
Sniping and copy-trade bots hit this constantly because their quote is stale by the time the transaction lands.
fix: Raise the max SOL input slightly and retry, accepting the higher entry price.
Reduce the token amount so the required SOL fits your current limit.
Add a priority fee so you land ahead of the price move rather than behind it.

entries.title: Too little SOL received to sell
entries.summary: Sell-side slippage: selling your tokens would return less SOL than your minimum. The curve dropped faster than your tolerance allowed.
why: The mirror image of 6002. Selling into a falling curve returns fewer lamports than min_sol_output.
Rugs and fast dumps move the curve down within one or two slots; a tight minimum rejects the fill.
It is the most common error bots see when dumping into their own price impact.
fix: Lower the minimum SOL output and retry, or sell a smaller amount so your own impact is smaller.
If you are exiting a collapsing coin, accept that the realized price will be well below the last quote.
Split the exit across several transactions instead of one market dump.

entries.title: The mint does not match the bonding curve
entries.summary: The mint account in the instruction is not the mint that the supplied bonding curve belongs to. A mismatched account pair.
why: Each bonding curve PDA is derived from one mint. Passing mint A with the curve of mint B is rejected outright.
It usually comes from a bot that builds instructions from a cached account set after the user switched tokens.
Copy-trading tools that reuse a template transaction and swap only the mint address trigger it constantly.
fix: Re-derive the bonding curve PDA from the mint you actually want to trade.
If a bot produced this, it is reusing another token's accounts — abandon it and use the official flow.
Verify in an explorer that the curve account's stored mint equals the mint you passed.

entries.title: Bonding curve complete
entries.summary: The coin already graduated: the curve filled, liquidity migrated to the AMM, and the curve no longer sells. This is the single most misread Pump.fun error.
why: Every launched coin trades on a bonding curve until it reaches the migration market cap. After that, the curve is closed and trading continues in a PumpSwap pool.
A transaction built against the old curve — especially one quoted seconds before graduation — has nothing left to trade against.
The on-chain message still says 'migrated to raydium' for historical reasons; graduated coins now go to PumpSwap.
Note the collision: 6005 means 'not enough percent to 100' on Jupiter, 'exceeded slippage' on Raydium CPMM, and 'curve complete' here.
fix: Trade the same coin through its PumpSwap pool instead of the curve — the front-end usually switches automatically on refresh.
Re-quote: any route or bot pinned to the curve address will keep failing.
Your funds were never at risk; the transaction reverted atomically and only the fee was spent.

entries.title: The bonding curve has not completed
entries.summary: A migration or post-graduation instruction ran against a curve that has not finished filling yet.
why: Migration is only valid at or after the completion threshold. Calling it early is rejected.
Bots that pre-fire migrate transactions hoping to be first in the migration block hit this.
It also fires when someone confuses 'creator can migrate early' rules with the public path.
fix: Wait until the curve actually completes; the migrate instruction has nothing to do before that.
Do not pre-sign migrate transactions to fire early — they simply fail and cost the fee.
Trade on the curve normally; migration happens on its own when the threshold is crossed.

entries.title: The program is not initialized
entries.summary: The account the instruction depends on has not been created yet — usually a missing bonding curve or global config for that mint.
why: Trading requires the per-mint curve account. If the mint exists but was never launched through Pump.fun, that account does not exist.
It also appears when the global config account is wrong, so the program cannot find its own state.
A token that merely looks like a Pump.fun coin (same ticker, similar name) but launched elsewhere produces this.
fix: Confirm the mint was actually launched on Pump.fun — check that a bonding curve PDA exists for it.
If you are integrating, initialize the expected accounts first rather than assuming they exist.
For a token that launched elsewhere, use the venue it actually belongs to.

entries.title: Withdraw attempted too frequently
entries.summary: A creator-fee withdrawal was rate limited because another withdrawal for the same vault happened too recently.
why: Creator fee vaults are rate limited to stop spam withdrawals that would each cost the vault rent.
Running collect twice in quick succession — or a bot retrying on timeout — trips the limiter.
The first withdrawal probably succeeded; the retry is what failed.
fix: Check the vault balance and transaction history before retrying — the earlier withdrawal likely went through.
Wait out the rate-limit window rather than hammering the call.
For bots, treat the rate-limit error as success-with-backoff, not as a retryable failure.

entries.title: Buy zero amount
entries.summary: The instruction asked to buy zero tokens. A computed amount rounded to zero before submission.
why: Bots that size trades as a fraction of balance can compute zero when the balance is tiny or a decimal conversion is wrong.
Sending an empty amount is rejected rather than treated as a no-op.
Front-ends with a minimum order size can also produce this when the input field is left blank.
fix: Enter a non-zero amount; check decimals so a UI value of 1 does not become 0 base units.
If a bot computed this, raise its minimum order size or skip rather than sending a zero trade.
Confirm the token's decimals before sizing — a 9-decimal token needs 10^9 per whole unit.

entries.title: Not enough tokens to buy
entries.summary: The curve does not have enough remaining tokens to fill the requested buy size. The coin is close to graduating and nearly sold out.
why: Each curve holds a fixed token supply. A large buy near the end of the curve cannot be filled from what remains.
It signals imminent graduation: the remaining supply is smaller than your order.
Bots that size by SOL rather than by remaining tokens hit it in the final stretch.
fix: Reduce the buy size to fit the remaining curve supply, or wait for graduation and buy from the AMM pool.
Refresh the curve state to see the actual remaining tokens rather than assuming the original supply.
If you are sniping late, understand you are competing for the last few percent of the curve.

entries.title: Not enough tokens to sell
entries.summary: You asked to sell more tokens than the curve can absorb, or more than you hold in the account passed in.
why: The sell must draw from your token account. A balance smaller than the amount — after fees or a prior partial sell — fails here.
Very large sells against thin curves exhaust the SOL side and cannot be absorbed in one instruction.
It also fires when the wrong token account is passed (a different mint's ATA).
fix: Check your actual token balance in that account and sell no more than it holds.
Split a large exit into several sells so the curve can absorb each one.
Confirm you passed the ATA for this specific mint, not a lookalike token account.

entries.title: Not enough SOL to cover rent exemption
entries.summary: Your wallet does not have enough SOL to create the associated token account for this coin on top of the trade itself.
why: The first buy of a new coin must create its associated token account, which requires rent-exempt lamports (~0.00204 SOL) in addition to the trade amount and fee.
A wallet funded with exactly the trade amount, or a fresh wallet sweeping all SOL, fails this check.
It is common for first-time buyers funding from an exchange with a round number.
fix: Add a small SOL buffer (0.01 SOL is plenty) and retry — this is not lost, it stays in your wallet as balance.
If you are emptying a wallet, leave enough for rent plus the network fee.
Once the token account exists, later buys of the same coin do not need this buffer again.

entries.title: Not enough SOL to cover fees
entries.summary: The wallet cannot cover the protocol fee plus the network fee for this buy. Distinct from 6040, which is about rent.
why: Pump.fun charges a trading fee on top of the Solana base and priority fee. A wallet sized to the trade amount alone comes up short.
It appears most on maximum-balance buys, where the user spends everything and leaves nothing for fees.
Priority fees rising during congestion can push an otherwise sufficient balance over the edge.
fix: Leave a fee buffer in the wallet rather than spending the entire balance on the trade.
Lower the priority fee if you set it manually and the network is not congested.
If you are trading from a fresh wallet, fund it with a little more than the intended trade size.

entries.title: Slippage: would buy less than min_tokens_out
entries.summary: Your minimum token output was not met — the buy would deliver fewer tokens than you required. The buy-side twin of a slippage limit, expressed in tokens rather than SOL.
why: A buy specifies both a SOL input and a minimum token output. When the curve price rises, the same SOL buys fewer tokens and the minimum fails.
This is what most sniping bots hit on a fast-moving launch: their minimum was calibrated to a price that no longer exists.
It is the same underlying condition as 6002, but the limit that broke was the token side rather than the SOL side.
fix: Lower min_tokens_out, or raise the SOL input so the same minimum is reachable.
Retry with a fresh quote rather than a recalculated one from an old price.
On a launch that is moving fast, accept that a tight minimum will simply miss the fill.

entries.title: Name too long
entries.summary: The token name exceeds the length limit the program stores. A launch-time validation error.
why: Coin metadata is stored on-chain in fixed-size fields. The name must fit the allocated space.
Long names with emoji or unusual Unicode can exceed the byte limit even when the character count looks short.
Launch tooling that does not truncate before submitting produces this.
fix: Shorten the name — count bytes, not characters; emoji and CJK characters take several bytes each.
Trim to a plain ASCII name if the launch keeps failing.
If using a launch bot, check whether it enforces the limit before building the transaction.

entries.title: Symbol too long
entries.summary: The ticker symbol exceeds the program's field length. Same family as the name limit, applied to the symbol.
why: The symbol field has its own fixed byte budget, smaller than the name field.
Multi-byte characters in a ticker consume the budget faster than they appear to.
Launch UIs usually truncate, but custom scripts often do not.
fix: Use a short ASCII ticker (a handful of characters is the practical norm).
Avoid emoji and non-Latin characters in the symbol.
Validate length client-side before submitting so the fee is not wasted.

entries.title: Uri too long
entries.summary: The metadata URI stored on-chain exceeds the allowed length. Commonly caused by an inline data URI instead of a hosted metadata link.
why: The URI field is fixed-size. A pointer to hosted JSON fits; a base64-encoded image embedded in the URI does not.
Launch tools that inline metadata to avoid a hosting dependency hit this immediately.
Very long query strings or tracking parameters can also push a normal link over the limit.
fix: Host the metadata JSON at a short URL and pass that link instead of inlining the data.
Strip tracking parameters from the URI before submitting.
If you need deep metadata, store it behind the link rather than in the on-chain field.

entries.title: Exceeded desired slippage limit
entries.summary: The pool's price crossed the limit you set, so the AMM refused the fill instead of executing at a worse rate. Nothing was swapped and only the network fee was spent.
why: The quote you signed and the state the pool had when the transaction landed were different. On a busy pair that gap is often more than the default 0.5% tolerance.
Your trade was large relative to the active liquidity, so your own order moved the price past the limit as it filled.
Someone swapped the same direction just ahead of you and shifted the price — the honest description of a sandwich, and also what ordinary bot competition looks like.
Direct integrations often compute minAmountOut once at quote time and reuse it across retries, which guarantees a stale limit.
fix: Refresh the quote and send again in the same minute. Most 0x1e failures succeed on the second attempt with no setting change at all.
If it keeps failing, raise tolerance one step (0.5% → 1.0% for majors, 1% → 2% for thin pairs). Do not jump to 10%: that is how you get filled at a bad price on purpose.
Split a large order into several smaller swaps so each one stays inside the pool's comfortable depth.
Attach a priority fee so the transaction lands in the next block instead of ageing in the queue while the price walks away.

entries.title: Insufficient funds
entries.summary: The AMM checked a vault balance and found less than the amount the instruction wanted to move. The shortfall can be in the pool's vault or in the source account you passed.
why: The pool has been drained below the requested output by trades that landed before yours, and your minAmountOut no longer fits what is left.
You are swapping the wrong direction: asking for token A while your source account holds token B produces the same message.
A wrapping step was skipped, so the WSOL account the AMM tried to debit was empty even though your wallet showed SOL.
The pool account list came from a cache and points at a vault that has since been replaced.
fix: Re-fetch the pool from the Raydium API and rebuild the transaction — do not reuse an account list across sessions.
Check the balance of the exact token account the swap debits, not the wallet's aggregate balance in the UI.
For SOL pairs, confirm the wrapped SOL account exists and holds the amount you are swapping before the swap instruction runs.
If you are integrating, read pool reserves immediately before building the instruction and size the trade to what is actually there.

entries.title: Invalid input
entries.summary: A parameter failed one of the AMM's range checks before any transfer happened — most often a zero amount, or a maximum-input that is smaller than the quoted amount.
why: The amount rounded to zero because the UI applied the wrong mint decimals (a 6-decimal token treated as 9).
maxAmountIn was derived from a stale quote and is now below the amount the swap actually needs.
A direct integration passed the swap parameters in the wrong order, so the program read the minimum-out value as an input amount.
Fee or status parameters are outside the allowed range on a pool created by a fork with different constants.
fix: Print the raw instruction arguments (lamport or base-unit integers, not UI decimals) and confirm none of them is zero.
Verify the mint decimals on chain with getMint, not from a token list — decimal drift is the single most common cause.
Recompute maxAmountIn from a fresh quote each time instead of reusing a stored value.
For custom integrations, decode the pool state first and mirror the official SDK's field order.

entries.title: Calculation exchange rate failed
entries.summary: The price calculation could not produce a number: either a reserve used in the division was zero, or the result overflowed the fixed-point type.
why: One side of the pool holds zero after a full drain or an initialisation that never funded the vault.
The two mints have very different decimals and the amounts are extreme, so the intermediate product exceeds u128.
Pool state is corrupt or was written by a fork with different math, so the reserve fields do not match the vaults.
A dust-sized swap against a huge reserve floors to zero and the rate check rejects it.
fix: Check both vault balances on chain. If either is zero the pool is unusable — route to another pool instead of retrying.
Try a larger amount for dust-size swaps; the AMM needs the rate to survive integer rounding.
Compare the pool account against a freshly fetched one; if reserves disagree with vault balances, the pool is broken.
Pick a different venue for extreme-decimal pairs — thin custom pools are where this fires most.

entries.title: Invalid status
entries.summary: The pool's status flag does not allow the action you requested — the program tracks whether a pool is initialised, swap-only, or winding down, and your instruction does not match it.
why: The pool is in a withdraw-only or deprecated state after a migration, so swaps are rejected while liquidity can still be pulled.
An admin changed the pool status between your quote and your transaction.
A forked deployment passes a status value the program does not recognise.
You are calling an instruction (deposit, withdraw) that the current status forbids even though the UI still shows the button.
fix: Read the pool's status field on chain and compare it with what the front-end assumes.
If the pool is deprecated, use the venue the liquidity migrated to — retrying will not change the answer.
For withdrawals, use the withdraw instruction the current status permits rather than the standard one.
Refresh the front-end; stale UIs keep offering actions the program has already disabled.

entries.title: Wrong accounts number
entries.summary: The instruction arrived with the wrong number of accounts. Raydium AMM v4 expects a fixed, ordered account list and validates its length before reading anything.
why: A custom client copied the account list from an older program version that had a different count.
Optional accounts (target orders, market-related) were omitted, shifting every later account by one position.
An SDK version mismatch: the client is newer than the on-chain program, or the reverse.
Someone hand-built the transaction and forgot the OpenBook market accounts.
fix: Use the official SDK to build the instruction — it encodes the exact account order for the deployed program version.
If you build manually, compare your list against a transaction that succeeded on the same instruction and diff the keys in order.
Never omit optional accounts by truncating the list; pass the expected placeholders instead.
Pin the SDK and the program version together; upgrading one without the other is the usual source of this error.

entries.title: Invalid supply
entries.summary: The LP token supply does not match what the operation requires — either the mint's supply was changed outside the AMM, or the pool was initialised with a supply the program did not expect.
why: The LP mint still has a mint authority, so somebody minted LP tokens outside the pool and broke the accounting.
A migration or fork copied pool state without copying the matching LP supply.
Deposit or withdraw is being called on a pool whose LP mint was frozen or whose authority was revoked.
An integration passed the wrong LP mint account, so the supply check ran against an unrelated token.
fix: Verify the LP mint address belongs to this pool and that its supply equals the pool's recorded LP amount.
Check the mint's authorities: a live mint authority on an AMM LP mint is a red flag for the pool's health.
If the pool was migrated, use the new pool rather than the old one whose LP accounting no longer closes.
Treat a persistent invalid supply as a reason to exit liquidity, not to retry.

entries.title: Expected mint
entries.summary: A token account was passed where a mint account is required. The program checks the account's data shape and rejects a balance-holding account in a mint slot.
why: Account order in the instruction is off by one, a very common result of mixing SDK versions.
A UI or script passed the user's token account instead of the mint when building a custom instruction.
The pool was created with a different mint layout than the client assumes, for example a Token-2022 mint.
You are reusing a transaction template that was written for a different pair.
fix: List the accounts in the failing instruction with their roles and confirm every mint slot holds a mint (data length 82, or the Token-2022 length).
Rebuild with the official SDK rather than patching a template.
For Token-2022 pools, check that the mint account is the Token-2022 one and not a legacy SPL mint with a similar name.
Log the account keys in the order the program received them; the mismatch is almost always visible immediately.

entries.title: Invalid target owner
entries.summary: The target-orders account is not owned by the authority the pool expects. Target orders hold the pool's OpenBook order state and must belong to this specific pool.
why: The target orders account was derived for a different pool or market and pasted into the transaction.
A pool was forked and the target orders account was recreated without updating the pool's recorded owner.
The pool predates a program upgrade that changed how target orders ownership is validated.
A client cached the account list from another pool on the same market.
fix: Derive the target orders PDA from this pool's program ID and pool state instead of copying it from another pool.
Fetch the pool account and read the target orders key it records; pass exactly that.
If you are not touching order-based liquidity, use a route that does not require target orders at all.
On old pools, verify against a known-good transaction before assuming your derivation is right.

entries.title: Invalid fee
