entries.summary: A fee parameter is outside the range the program accepts. This only comes from pool creation or fee administration, never from a normal swap.
why: Pool creation passed a numerator or denominator that makes the fee exceed the program's maximum.
An admin instruction tried to set a swap fee above the allowed ceiling.
A forked deployment reused fee constants that no longer match the program build.
The fee fields were written in the wrong unit (basis points versus a fixed-point fraction).
fix: Check the fee field's unit in the program source and convert accordingly before sending.
Stay inside the documented ceiling; a pool created above it cannot be corrected later without admin rights.
For users seeing this during a swap, the front-end is sending an admin instruction — reload it and use the normal flow.
If you forked the program, re-derive the constants from your own build rather than copying the upstream ones.

entries.title: Lamports calculate error
entries.summary: The SOL side of the accounting did not add up: the lamport balance of the wrapped-SOL account or the pool's fee account was not what the program expected at settlement.
why: The WSOL account was closed, drained, or had its rent-exempt minimum moved during the same transaction.
Another instruction in the same transaction spent lamports the AMM was counting on.
A SOL-pair swap was built without the wrap instruction, so the account had less than the amount being swapped.
Rent-exempt edge cases on a freshly created account leave one lamport less than the program requires.
fix: Build SOL swaps with the standard wrap → swap → unwrap sequence and keep those instructions adjacent.
Do not bundle transfers that touch the same WSOL account in the same transaction as the swap.
Check the WSOL account's lamport balance immediately before the swap instruction runs.
If you assemble transactions yourself, keep the rent-exempt minimum untouched and only spend the swap amount.

entries.title: Checked subtraction overflow
entries.summary: An arithmetic subtraction went below zero and the checked math aborted the instruction. On a healthy pool this is impossible, so treat it as a signal about the pool, not about your wallet.
why: The pool's reserves were pushed near zero by a large trade or a drain, so the amount being subtracted exceeds what remains.
Pool state was written by a fork with different math, leaving reserves inconsistent with the vaults.
An integration requested an output larger than the reserve because minAmountOut came from a different pool.
Extreme decimal mismatches between the two mints produce intermediate values that overflow the adjacent additions and multiplications (codes 0x21–0x23).
fix: Do not retry. Fetch the pool reserves and confirm they match the on-chain vault balances first.
If the reserves disagree with the vaults, the pool is broken — route elsewhere.
Right-size the trade: request no more than a small fraction of the smaller reserve.
Report the pool if you are the integrator; overflow on a functioning pool usually means a state bug worth flagging.

entries.title: Token min subceeded
entries.summary: An exact-input swap produced less output than your minimum. Orca's name for the everyday slippage rejection, and the most common Whirlpool failure by a wide margin.
why: Price moved between the quote and the fill. Concentrated liquidity makes this happen faster than on a constant-product pool because liquidity thins out between ticks.
Your trade crossed many ticks, so each step filled at a slightly worse price than the average you were quoted.
The transaction landed two or three blocks later than expected because the priority fee was too low for the current congestion.
tokenMin was hardcoded in an integration instead of being derived from the live quote.
fix: Retry with a fresh quote first; most of these clear on the next attempt.
Widen slippage one step. On Whirlpools the useful range is narrower than on AMMs: 0.5% to 1% for deep pools, 2% to 3% for thin ones.
Add a priority fee; the failure is often just latency, not price.
Split the trade so it stops at a tick boundary instead of eating through several price levels in one fill.

entries.title: Exceeded token max
entries.summary: An exact-output swap needed more input than the maximum you allowed. The mirror image of 6018: here you fixed the amount you want out, so the variable is what you pay in.
why: The price worsened between quote and execution, and because the output was fixed the program had to pull more input to reach it.
A 'swap for exactly X tokens' flow was used on a volatile pair where the input cost moves quickly.
tokenMax was computed from a quote that is now stale.
Thin concentrated liquidity meant the last portion of the trade filled at a much worse rate, pushing total input over the cap.
fix: Re-quote and retry; exact-output swaps need fresher data than exact-input ones.
Raise the input cap slightly, or switch the flow to exact-input if the exact output amount is not essential.
Avoid exact-output on low-liquidity pools — the input side is the one that moves.
If you are integrating, pass tokenMax as a computed ceiling from the quote plus tolerance, not as a fixed number.

entries.title: Amount out below minimum
entries.summary: The output amount fell under the minimum threshold, including any transfer fee the mint charges. Shows up on exact-input swaps against token mints that withhold a fee on transfer.
why: The mint charges a transfer fee through Token-2022, and the fee is deducted from what actually arrives, so the post-fee amount drops under the threshold.
The pool is fee-tiered, and the tier's fee was not included when the minimum was computed.
Price moved as usual between quote and fill.
An integration compared the pre-fee output with a post-fee minimum.
fix: Compute the minimum on the post-fee amount when the output mint has a transfer fee extension.
Check the mint's fee basis points on chain (getMint with extensions enabled) before choosing a threshold.
Raise slippage slightly to absorb the fee, or route through a venue that reports post-fee quotes.
If you are integrating, use the SDK's fee-aware amount helpers instead of plain arithmetic.

entries.title: Amount in above maximum
entries.summary: The input amount exceeded the maximum you allowed, again accounting for transfer fees. Fires on exact-output swaps where the input is the free variable.
why: Price moved against you and the fixed output now costs more than the cap.
A transfer-fee mint is on the input side, so the amount the pool receives differs from the amount debited from your account.
The cap was set from a quote denominated before fees.
Large trade relative to available liquidity in the current tick range.
fix: Re-quote, then resend with a cap derived from that quote plus tolerance.
Add the input mint's transfer fee to your cap calculation.
Reduce the requested output so the required input fits your budget.
Prefer exact-input flows when the input amount is what you actually care about.

entries.title: Price outside slippage bounds
entries.summary: The pool's current price sits outside the bounds implied by your slippage setting and the price limit you passed, so the swap was rejected before execution.
why: The sqrt-price limit in the instruction is on the wrong side of the current price for the direction you are swapping.
Slippage was set so tight that the allowed band no longer contains the pool's price after a small move.
A stale pool object was used, so the price the client assumed differs from the chain's.
Pools with adaptive fees tighten these bounds dynamically in volatile markets.
fix: Let the SDK compute the sqrt-price limit from the current pool price and your slippage, rather than passing a stored value.
Re-fetch pool state immediately before building the transaction.
Loosen slippage for pairs with adaptive or dynamic fees; the effective band is narrower than the nominal percentage suggests.
Check the swap direction flag matches the price limit you pass.

entries.title: Tick array index out of bounds
entries.summary: The tick arrays passed for the swap do not cover the range the trade needs, or the array index does not exist for this pool's tick spacing.
why: A cached tick-array list was reused after the price moved into a region not covered by those arrays.
The array index was computed with the wrong tick spacing — each Whirlpool fixes its spacing at creation and the index depends on it.
The trade is large enough to cross more tick arrays than were supplied.
A pool was recreated with different parameters, so old array addresses no longer exist.
fix: Fetch the tick arrays for the current price and the direction of the swap right before sending.
Read tickSpacing from the pool and derive the array index with that value.
Supply enough arrays for the trade size, or reduce the size so it stays within the arrays you have.
Never persist tick-array addresses across sessions.

entries.title: Invalid tick array sequence
entries.summary: The tick arrays were supplied, but not in the order the swap requires. Whirlpools reads them sequentially from the current price toward the trade direction and checks adjacency.
why: Arrays were sorted ascending regardless of swap direction; a B-to-A swap needs them in descending order.
One array in the middle is missing, so the sequence has a gap.
An SDK built the sequence from a pool snapshot, then the price moved across a boundary before landing.
Mixed array sets from two different fetches were concatenated.
fix: Use the SDK's tick-array sequence builder; it handles direction and adjacency for you.
If you build it manually, start from the array containing the current tick and walk in the swap direction.
Fetch all arrays in one pass so they are consistent with each other.
After a large price move, discard the sequence and rebuild it.

entries.title: There are no tradable amount to swap
entries.summary: The swap resolved to zero tradable liquidity: either the amount is dust, or there is no initialised liquidity in the price range the trade would touch.
why: The pool has liquidity only in narrow ranges far from the current price, so the active range is effectively empty.
The amount is so small that the output floors to zero after fees.
All liquidity on the relevant side was withdrawn by LPs a moment ago.
The pool is freshly created and no position has been opened yet.
fix: Increase the amount above the dust threshold; tiny swaps cannot survive fee rounding.
Check the pool's liquidity distribution before trading — a pool with no in-range position cannot fill anything.
Route to a different pool for this pair.
If you are an LP, deposit into the active range rather than a range the price never visits.

entries.title: This whirlpool only supports full-range positions
entries.summary: You tried to open a narrow position on a pool that was created with the full-range-only flag. Such pools accept one position shape and reject anything custom.
why: The pool was deliberately created for full-range liquidity, often to keep routing simple and price impact predictable.
The position range in the instruction does not equal the pool's full tick range.
A UI offered a custom range picker that this pool's program path does not support.
An integration reused position-building code written for a normal pool.
fix: Open the position with the pool's minimum and maximum tick indexes instead of a custom range.
Use the standard full-range deposit flow the front-end offers for this pool.
If you specifically want concentrated liquidity, choose a pool that is not full-range-only.
Integrators: read the pool's flag before showing a range selector.

entries.title: Token mint has unsupported attributes
entries.summary: The mint uses Token-2022 extensions the Whirlpool program does not handle, such as non-transferable or confidential balances, so the pool refuses to trade it.
why: The token is non-transferable, which makes a swap structurally impossible.
Confidential transfer or confidential mint-burn extensions are enabled.
A transfer hook is configured but the calling flow does not supply the hook accounts.
A newer extension was enabled on the mint after the pool was created.
fix: Check the mint's extensions on chain; if it is non-transferable, no DEX can trade it.
For transfer-hook mints, use the pool via a route that passes the hook accounts (see 6050).
Pick a pool that was created for this mint's extension set.
If you are the issuer, be aware that enabling certain extensions after launch kills DEX tradability.

entries.title: Unable to call transfer hook without extra accounts
entries.summary: The token mint runs a transfer hook, and the swap did not pass the extra accounts that hook needs. Token-2022 requires the hook's accounts on every transfer.
why: The mint has the transfer-hook extension and the pool's swap instruction must forward the hook's accounts as remaining accounts.
An aggregator or custom client built the swap without discovering the hook's required account list.
The hook program was added to the mint after the route was cached.
Extra accounts were passed but in the wrong order or for the wrong mint side.
fix: Fetch the hook's extra-account-metas PDA and append the accounts it lists to the swap instruction.
Use an SDK version that supports transfer-hook mints end to end rather than patching the account list by hand.
If your wallet or router does not support hooks, use a router that does.
Verify the accounts are appended for the token that actually carries the hook.

entries.title: Position is not empty, it cannot be closed
entries.summary: The position still holds liquidity or uncollected fees and rewards, so it cannot be closed yet. Closing is only allowed when the position is fully withdrawn and harvested.
why: Liquidity was not removed before the close instruction.
Fees or rewards accrued after the withdraw and were never collected.
A partial withdraw left a dust amount of liquidity behind.
The close instruction was sent in the same transaction as the withdraw, but ordered before it.
fix: Call decrease-liquidity with the full position liquidity, then collect fees and rewards, then close.
Check the position's liquidity and owed-fee fields before sending close.
Order the instructions withdraw → collect → close within the transaction.
If dust remains, withdraw the remaining liquidity exactly rather than rounding.

entries.title: Liquidity amount must be greater than zero
entries.summary: The deposit computed to zero liquidity. The amounts you supplied are too small relative to the position's price range to mint any liquidity units.
why: Deposit amounts are dust relative to the range width and the pool's current price.
The range is so narrow that the liquidity formula rounds down to zero.
Only one side of the pair was funded, and at this price that side contributes nothing.
Decimal mismatch made a seemingly normal amount arrive as a tiny integer.
fix: Increase the deposit amount, or widen the price range so the same amount buys liquidity.
Fund both tokens in the ratio the range requires; the UI's suggested ratio is usually right.
Confirm the amounts are in base units with the correct decimals.
If you only want one-sided exposure, use a range that actually sits on one side of the current price.

entries.title: Trade is not enabled yet
entries.summary: The pool exists but its trading start time has not arrived. Whirlpools can be initialised ahead of a launch and reject swaps until the configured timestamp passes.
why: The pool was created with a trade-enable timestamp in the future, a common pattern for scheduled launches.
Your clock and the cluster's clock differ enough that the UI thinks trading is open.
The pool's enable time was pushed back by the creator after you loaded the page.
You are hitting the pool a few seconds early on a launch with bots competing.
fix: Wait until the stated enable time, then retry — nothing is wrong with your wallet.
Refresh the page after the launch time instead of retrying against a cached state.
On launch pools, expect the first blocks to fail with slippage rather than this error once trading opens.
Check the pool's enable timestamp on chain if you need the exact second.

entries.title: Exceeded amount slippage tolerance
entries.summary: The total output of the swap fell below your minimum, or the required input rose above your maximum. The ordinary slippage rejection, measured on the whole trade rather than per price step.
why: DLMM fills bin by bin, and each bin has its own price, so a large trade walks the price down in visible steps and can overshoot your limit.
Liquidity is concentrated in a few bins; once those are consumed the price jumps to the next populated bin.
The quote was taken before a burst of activity in the same direction.
Your minimum was computed on the mid price rather than on the expected fill including price impact.
fix: Re-quote and retry; DLMM pools change shape quickly as LPs move ranges.
Raise tolerance one step, but keep it tight on bin pools — a 5% tolerance on a wide-bin pool can be a genuinely bad fill.
Reduce the size so the trade stays within one or two bins.
Use the SDK's quote, which simulates the bin walk, instead of computing output from reserves.

entries.title: Exceeded bin slippage tolerance
entries.summary: The swap would have crossed more bins than your maximum. DLMM lets you cap how far the price is allowed to walk, independently of the amount-based slippage limit.
why: maxBinToCross was set too low for the trade size, so the program stopped before filling anything.
The active bin moved away from your quote, leaving empty bins between the price and the liquidity you wanted.
A wallet or SDK defaulted the bin cap to a small number for safety.
You are swapping a token whose liquidity sits in a distant range, so reaching it requires crossing many empty bins.
fix: Raise maxBinToCross to what the route actually needs — the SDK's quote returns the number of bins it will cross.
If the required bin count is very large, the pool is illiquid for your size; use a smaller trade or another venue.
Re-quote right before sending so the cap matches current liquidity placement.
Do not raise the cap blindly: it is your protection against filling through a long stretch of bad prices.

entries.title: Pair insufficient liquidity
entries.summary: There is not enough liquidity in the reachable bins to complete the swap, even allowing for slippage. The pool ran out of tokens on the side you are buying.
why: LPs concentrated liquidity far from the current price, so the reachable bins hold very little.
A large share of liquidity was withdrawn after your quote.
The trade is simply bigger than the pool's depth.
The active bin is at the edge of the populated range, so only one direction has liquidity.
fix: Reduce the amount until it fits the pool's depth; the quote shows the maximum fillable size.
Check the pool's bin distribution before trading — a pool with 90% of liquidity in a narrow band cannot absorb size.
Split the order or route through an aggregator that spans several pools.
If you are an LP, this is the signal that the pool needs liquidity in the active range.

entries.title: Zero liquidity
entries.summary: The liquidity amount computed to zero. The deposit is too small for the bin range, or the position has nothing left to withdraw.
why: Deposit amounts are dust compared with the bin's price scale, so the liquidity units round to zero.
The position was already fully withdrawn.
A single-bin deposit skipped the side of the pair that the bin actually needs.
Decimal mismatch turned a normal-looking amount into a tiny integer.
fix: Increase the deposit, or widen the bin range so the same funds produce liquidity.
Confirm the position's current liquidity before withdrawing.
Match the deposit ratio the bin requires — a single bin only needs one side at its price.
Verify base-unit amounts and mint decimals.

entries.title: Bin array not found
entries.summary: A bin array account the instruction needs does not exist on chain. DLMM stores bins in arrays of fixed size, and an array is only created when liquidity first reaches that range.
why: The target bin falls in a range where no LP has ever deposited, so its array was never initialised.
A cached array address was reused after a pool was recreated.
The array index was derived with the wrong bins-per-array constant.
A swap crossed into a bin range whose array was closed after all liquidity left.
fix: Re-fetch the bin arrays for the current active bin instead of reusing cached addresses.
Derive the array PDA from the pool address and index using the program's constant.
For deposits, choose a bin range whose arrays exist, or create the position through the SDK which handles array initialisation.
If a swap needs an uninitialised array, the price range is empty — route elsewhere.

entries.title: Invalid bin array
entries.summary: The bin array account passed does not belong to this pool, or its index does not match the bin being accessed. The program validates both the owner and the recorded index.
why: The array came from another pool on the same program — addresses look identical in shape.
Index and array were mismatched when assembling the account list by hand.
The pool's array set changed and a stale list was reused.
A forked deployment derived arrays with a different seed.
fix: Derive each array from this pool's address and the exact bin index.
Let the SDK build the array list; hand-assembly is where this error is born.
Log the array's recorded index and compare it with the bin you are targeting.
Discard cached arrays whenever the pool address changes.

entries.title: Bin arrays must be continuous
entries.summary: The bin arrays supplied have a gap: the ones needed for this operation must be consecutive so the program can walk from one to the next without missing a range.
why: One array in the middle was omitted because it holds no liquidity — but continuity is required regardless of whether a bin is empty.
Arrays were fetched in two separate calls and one of them was stale.
The account list was trimmed to save transaction size.
Swap direction requires a descending sequence and the list was sorted ascending.
fix: Pass every array between the start and end bin, including arrays with no liquidity.
Fetch the whole range in a single call so indices are consistent.
Use the SDK's sequence builder, which fills gaps automatically.
If the transaction is too large, reduce the trade so it spans fewer arrays.

entries.title: Position is not empty
entries.summary: The position still holds liquidity or fees, so it cannot be closed. DLMM requires a clean position before the account is reclaimed.
why: Withdraw was skipped or only partially executed.
Fees accrued in the bins after the withdraw instruction was built.
The close was sent before the withdraw in the same transaction.
A dust amount of liquidity remained because the withdraw amount was rounded.
fix: Remove all liquidity, claim fees, then close — in that order.
Check the position's liquidity fields before sending close.
Withdraw the exact remaining amount rather than a rounded figure.
Keep withdraw and close as separate steps if you are debugging ordering.

entries.title: Cannot find non-zero liquidity bin array id
entries.summary: The swap could not locate any bin array with liquidity in the direction it needs to trade. The populated range does not overlap the path from the active bin.
why: Liquidity sits entirely on one side of the active bin, so one swap direction has nothing to fill against.
LPs withdrew from the active range and left positions far away.
The pool is new and only partially seeded.
The swap amount and bin cap allow only a short walk that never reaches the populated range.
fix: Try the opposite direction, or reduce the bin cap requirement by re-quoting.
Inspect the pool's liquidity distribution and confirm there is depth near the active bin.
Use another pool for this pair if the distribution is one-sided.
As an LP, add liquidity around the active bin so both directions can trade.

entries.title: Insufficient out amount
entries.summary: The computed output is below the minimum you specified for an exact-input swap. DLMM's per-trade version of the slippage check, evaluated after the bin walk.
why: Price impact through the bins exceeded what your minimum allowed.
A quote was taken at a moment when the active bin held more liquidity than it does now.
Fees were not included when computing the minimum.
The trade is large relative to the number of populated bins.
fix: Re-quote, then retry with the minimum derived from that quote.
Use the SDK's simulation rather than a reserves-based estimate; DLMM output depends on bin placement.
Reduce size or raise tolerance slightly for thin pools.
Account for the pool's fee tier when setting the minimum.

entries.title: Pool disabled
entries.summary: The pool has been disabled by its operator. Swaps, and usually deposits, are rejected until it is re-enabled — this is a deliberate switch, not a failure of your transaction.
why: The pool's admin disabled it, typically during an incident review or before a migration.
The pool was flagged for suspicious activity or a configuration fix.
You are interacting with a pool that has been superseded by a replacement.
An abandoned fork left the flag set from testing.
fix: Use another pool for the pair; retrying will not succeed while the flag is set.
If you hold a position, check whether withdrawals remain permitted — usually they do.
Watch the operator's announcements for re-enable or migration instructions.
Integrators: check the disabled flag in pool state before routing to it.

entries.title: Swapped amount is exceeded max swapped amount
entries.summary: The swap is larger than the pool's configured per-transaction cap. DLMM pools can enforce a maximum swap size as an anti-manipulation guard.
why: The pool sets a cap relative to its liquidity so a single transaction cannot drain a range.
Your amount exceeds that cap after fees and bin walk are accounted for.
The cap was lowered by the operator after you last traded.
A routed order was combined into one swap that is larger than any single leg should be.
fix: Split the order into several swaps under the cap.
Route through an aggregator that splits across pools.
Read the pool's cap from state if you are integrating, and size legs accordingly.
Check whether the cap changed if your usual size suddenly fails.

entries.title: Bonding curve has already migrated
entries.summary: The coin finished its bonding curve and moved to the AMM, so the bonding-curve program no longer trades it. Buying or selling here can never succeed; the token now trades on the graduated pool.
why: The curve reached its funding target and liquidity was migrated, which is a one-way transition.
A cached trade route still points at the bonding curve after graduation.
The front-end did not refresh the coin's state, so the buy button still calls the curve.
A bot is racing the migration and keeps retrying the curve path.
fix: Reload the token page so the route switches to the graduated AMM pool, then trade there.
If you are integrating, check the bonding curve's complete flag before building the instruction.
Use the project's official AMM pool address after migration; liquidity lives there now.
Expect this error in the first seconds after graduation — it is a routing problem, not a loss.

entries.title: Account type not supported
entries.summary: An account was passed whose type tag does not match what this instruction expects. Pump tags its accounts (global, bonding curve, fee config, sharing config) and rejects a mismatch before doing any work.
why: A sharing-config or fee-config account was passed where a bonding curve was expected, a common mix-up in the newer instruction set.
The account list was assembled for a different instruction variant (v1 versus v2 versus v3).
A stale account from before a migration still carries the old type tag.
An SDK version older than the deployed program built the account list.
fix: Match the instruction variant to the account set: v2 and v3 trades take different remaining accounts.
Upgrade the client SDK so its account builders match the current program.
Fetch the account and read its type tag before passing it; the mismatch is visible in the first bytes.
When copying an account list from an explorer, confirm which instruction it belonged to.

entries.title: Sell zero amount
entries.summary: The sell amount arrived as zero. Either the UI rounded your whole balance away, or the token account you are selling from is empty.
why: The amount was computed in UI units and truncated to zero because of a decimals mismatch.
A 'sell all' flow read the balance before a pending buy settled, so it read zero.
You are selling from a different token account than the one holding the balance.
A dust balance below one base unit cannot be expressed at all.
fix: Refresh balances, then sell again — 'sell all' needs a settled balance to read.
Check the base-unit amount being passed; it must be a positive integer.
Confirm the token account that holds the tokens is the one in the instruction.
If the balance really is dust, it cannot be sold; the curve has a minimum tradable size.

entries.title: Overflow
entries.summary: A curve calculation overflowed the integer type. On a normal coin this is unreachable, so it points at an absurd amount, a corrupt curve account, or a fork with different constants.
why: The amount passed is far beyond any real balance, usually from a decimal or unit error in an integration.
The bonding curve's reserve fields were written by a different program version.
A token created with extreme supply parameters pushes intermediate products past the type limit.
A custom build reused the program with different constants and did not re-check the bounds.
fix: Verify the amount is in base units and within the total supply.
Do not retry with a larger amount; that makes it worse.
If you are the integrator, decode the curve account and confirm reserves are sane.
Report the coin if a normal-sized trade overflows — the curve state is likely broken.

entries.title: Not enough remaining accounts
entries.summary: The instruction expects extra accounts beyond the fixed list — creator vault, fee recipients, or sharing-config accounts — and not enough were supplied.
why: Creator fee and buyback flows require a variable set of remaining accounts that the client must append.
A fee-sharing coin needs one account per shareholder; the client passed the default set only.
The coin was updated to a sharing config after the client cached its account list.
Multi-hop or quote-chain trades need one account per hop.
fix: Fetch the coin's current fee configuration and append the exact accounts it lists, in order.
Upgrade the SDK; older versions do not know about sharing-config accounts.
For fee-sharing coins, the remaining accounts must match the shareholder count exactly.
If the count keeps changing, the coin's config is being edited — reload and rebuild.

entries.title: Create v2 disabled
entries.summary: The create-v2 instruction is switched off right now. The program has a switch for the newer creation path, and when it is off only the original create flow works.
why: The operator disabled the newer creation path, usually while a feature is rolled out or paused.
The feature is only enabled on certain clusters or ramp schedules.
A client hardcoded create-v2 because it supports a newer feature set.
A fork of the program never enabled it.
fix: Use the original create flow, which remains available.
Wait for the feature to be re-enabled if create-v2 features are essential to you.
Upgrade the client so it can fall back automatically instead of failing hard.
Check the program's config account to see which creation paths are live.

entries.title: Cashback is not enabled
entries.summary: You tried to trade a cashback coin through a path where cashback is not active — either the coin does not carry the flag, or the instruction variant you used does not support it.
why: The coin was created without the cashback flag, so cashback accounts have nothing to credit.
A v2 instruction was used without the cashback remaining accounts.
The cashback feature is disabled globally for new coins while older coins keep the flag.
An SDK assumed cashback from the coin's name or UI badge rather than its on-chain flag.
fix: Use the standard trade instruction for coins without the cashback flag.
For cashback coins, pass the accumulator and recipient accounts the v2 path expects.
Read the coin's flag on chain instead of inferring it from the UI.
If the feature is globally disabled for new coins, no workaround exists for new creations.

entries.title: Unsupported quote mint
entries.summary: The coin is priced in a quote mint the program does not accept. The newer curve types allow coins quoted in tokens other than SOL, but only from a whitelist.
why: The quote mint is not on the program's whitelist, so no bonding curve can be created or traded against it.
A create-v2 request used a token that looks like a common quote asset but is a different mint.
The whitelist changed after the coin was created.
A forked deployment has its own whitelist that does not include the mint.
fix: Check the whitelist before creating a quote-paired coin; only listed mints work.
Confirm the quote mint address character by character — spoof tokens copy the symbol, not the address.
For existing coins, trade through the quote asset the curve was actually created with.
If you fork the program, seed your own whitelist.

entries.title: Cashback coins can no longer be created
entries.summary: New cashback coins are no longer accepted. Coins that already carry the flag keep working, but creation with cashback is closed.
why: The feature was retired for new creations, which is a program-level switch.
A client still offers a cashback toggle that the program now rejects.
A fork copied the flag handling without the retirement check.
Documentation or tutorials predate the retirement.
fix: Create the coin without the cashback flag.
For existing cashback coins, keep using the v2 trade path they require.
Update the client so the toggle disappears instead of failing at send time.
Do not build new products on a retired creation feature.

entries.title: v3 trades do not support cashback coins
entries.summary: The v3 trade instruction cannot handle cashback coins. Cashback coins must be traded through the v2 instructions, which carry the accumulator accounts.
why: The coin carries the cashback flag, but the client used the v3 trade path.
A router upgraded to v3 globally and did not branch on the coin's flag.
Mixed instruction versions within one route, which the program rejects.
An SDK chose v3 by default for all coins.
fix: Branch on the coin's cashback flag and use v2 for cashback coins, v3 otherwise.
Route cashback coins through a client that supports both variants.
If you are integrating, keep both instruction builders available instead of replacing one with the other.
Check the coin's flag after any config change on the bonding curve.

entries.title: Quote curve is complete but not yet migrated
entries.summary: The coin is priced in a quote token, and that quote side's curve is complete but not migrated yet. Trading is paused until the migration instruction runs.
why: Quote-chain coins have two curves: the coin's own and the quote asset's. Both must be usable for a trade.
The quote curve hit its target and is waiting for its migration step.
Only one of the two migration instructions was sent, leaving the pair half-migrated.
A bot is hammering the curve during the migration window.
fix: Wait a short while and retry — migration usually completes within a few blocks once triggered.
Do not send repeated trades during the window; they all fail the same way.
If you are the integrator, check the quote curve's migration state before routing.
For projects running the migration yourself, send the migrate instruction for the quote side.

entries.title: Quote chain accounts required
entries.summary: The quote coin is itself a pump coin, so the trade needs the quote side's bonding-curve account as a remaining account. Without it the program cannot price the second hop.
why: Nested quote coins require one bonding-curve account per quote hop.
The client treated the trade as a simple SOL pair and sent no extra accounts.
A multi-hop route was assembled without the quote chain's accounts.
The coin's quote configuration changed after the client cached the account list.
fix: Append the quote coin's bonding-curve account (and vault accounts) as remaining accounts.
Use an SDK version that understands quote-chain coins.
Count the hops in the quote chain and pass one curve account for each.
Re-fetch the coin's quote configuration before building the route.

entries.title: Mint required for this account to transfer tokens
entries.summary: The mint charges a transfer fee, so a transfer must include the mint account and state the expected fee. A plain transfer cannot work on a fee-enabled mint.
why: The mint has the transfer-fee extension, and the fee can only be computed with the mint's fee state in the account list.
A wallet or program used transfer instead of transfer_checked_with_fee.
The mint account was omitted to save transaction space.
A fork of an older integration predates the fee extension.
fix: Use transfer_checked_with_fee and pass the mint plus the expected fee.
If you are the sender and only need to move tokens, use a wallet or SDK that supports Token-2022 fees.
Compute the fee from the mint's fee configuration so the expected value matches.
Never strip the mint account from a transfer on a Token-2022 mint.

entries.title: Transferring, minting, and burning is paused on this mint
entries.summary: The issuer pressed pause. The pausable extension can stop transfers, minting and burning in one switch, and every instruction that moves tokens is rejected while it is on.
why: The mint's pause authority paused the mint, deliberately or during an incident.
A DEX swap fails because the swap's internal transfer hits the same switch.
The pause was applied after your quote but before your transaction landed.
A token project paused trading ahead of an announcement or migration.
fix: Wait for the issuer to resume; there is no user-side workaround.
Check the mint's pause state before retrying, so you are not burning fees on guaranteed failures.
If you hold a position in a pool with this token, expect withdrawals to fail as well while paused.
Treat a long pause as a counterparty risk decision, not a technical problem.

entries.title: Transfer fee exceeds maximum
entries.summary: The configured transfer fee is above the protocol ceiling of 10,000 basis points. This only comes from mint initialisation or a fee update, never from a normal transfer.
why: Initialisation passed a fee in the wrong unit, so a 1% fee was written as 100%.
A fee update tried to exceed the ceiling.
A forked program reused constants that differ from the deployed build.
An SDK serialised basis points as a fraction.
fix: Convert to basis points: 1% is 100, the ceiling is 10,000.
Check the fee update authority before attempting changes.
If you are a user seeing this, the issuer's tooling is misconfigured — nothing on your side will fix it.
For forks, re-derive the ceiling from your own build.

entries.title: CPI Guard blocked a transfer
entries.summary: The account has CPI Guard enabled, and a program tried to move its tokens without an approved delegate. The guard exists to stop malicious programs from draining accounts through CPI.
why: The wallet enabled CPI Guard on this token account, which blocks program-initiated transfers.
A DEX or staking program pulls tokens via CPI and the user never approved it as a delegate.
A delegated transfer expired or was revoked.
The program used a plain transfer instead of the delegate path.
fix: Approve the program as a delegate for the exact amount, then retry.
If you do not trust the program, do not disable the guard — use a different route.
Disable CPI Guard only for accounts you actively trade from, and understand that it lowers your protection.
Integrators: use the delegate flow, not a direct CPI transfer, for guarded accounts.

entries.title: Calculated fee does not match expected fee
entries.summary: You told the program what the transfer fee would be, and its calculation disagreed. The expected fee is a safety check: if it does not match, the transfer is refused rather than silently overcharging.
why: The fee was computed from a stale mint state, before the fee was updated.
Rounding differences between the client's formula and the program's integer math.
The fee was calculated on the pre-fee amount instead of the transferred amount.
The mint's fee changed between quote and send.
fix: Re-read the mint's fee configuration and recompute with the program's rounding (floor).
Use the SDK's fee helper rather than reimplementing the formula.
Retry after the fee update settles; the mismatch is often a race.
When in doubt, pass the maximum fee the extension reports and let the program compute the exact value.

entries.title: Extension type does not match existing extensions
entries.summary: An instruction tried to add or reallocate an extension whose type conflicts with what the account already holds. Extensions are typed and cannot be swapped after initialisation.
why: The account was initialised with one extension and the instruction targets another.
A reallocate used the wrong extension discriminator.
A closed and reopened account still holds the old extension layout.
Two tools each tried to initialise a different extension on the same account.
fix: Read the account's extension list (getAccountInfo with the Token-2022 parser) before adding anything.
Match the extension type to the one already present.
If you need a different extension, create a new account; you cannot convert in place.
Close and recreate only after withdrawing balances and fees.

entries.title: Extension already initialized on this account
entries.summary: The extension was initialised twice. This is idempotency protection: the second call is refused rather than overwriting configuration someone may be relying on.
why: A retry sent the initialise instruction again after the first one already succeeded.
A front-end ran initialisation on page load, so a refresh repeated it.
An integration assumed failure when the first attempt timed out, but it had actually landed.
Two instructions in the same transaction both initialise the same extension.
fix: Check the account's extensions first; if it is already set up, skip the instruction.
Confirm on an explorer whether the earlier transaction actually landed before retrying.
Make initialisation idempotent in your client: read, then conditionally initialise.
Never bundle two initialisers for the same extension.

entries.title: No authority exists to perform the desired operation
entries.summary: The operation needs an authority the mint or account no longer has. Extensions such as transfer fees require authorities, and revoking them makes certain changes permanently impossible.
why: The fee or pause authority was revoked, and the instruction needs it.
The mint was created without the authority the extension requires.
A multisig authority was expected but the signer set did not include it.
The authority was transferred to another key after the client cached the old one.
fix: Read the mint's authority fields and confirm which key can still act.
If the authority was revoked, the operation is permanently closed — no workaround exists.
Use the multisig flow if the authority is a multisig.
Before creating a mint, decide deliberately which authorities to keep and which to revoke.

entries.title: Transfer is disabled for this mint
entries.summary: The mint is non-transferable. Tokens can be minted and burned but never moved between accounts, which makes any swap or DEX pool structurally impossible.
why: The issuer enabled the non-transferable extension, often for credentials or receipts.
A token was created as a soulbound-style asset and later listed on a DEX anyway.
A pool was created for a mint whose extension state changed afterwards.
A fork or wrapper tried to move the token through CPI.
fix: There is no fix: non-transferable means non-transferable by design.
If you need transferability, the issuer must create a new mint — this one cannot be changed.
Do not attempt to wrap it into a transferable token expecting a DEX listing to work.
For issuers: decide transferability before minting; it is not reversible.

entries.title: Extension not found in account data
entries.summary: An instruction or client read asked for an extension the account does not have. The account's stored layout has no such type, so there is nothing to read or update.
why: The extension was expected but never initialised on this particular account.
An instruction targeted the mint's extension when the account-level one was meant, or the reverse.
The account is an older layout created before the extension existed.
A clone of a mint copied the address expectation but not the layout.
fix: Parse the account and list its extensions before calling an extension-specific instruction.
Initialise the extension first, then call the instruction that needs it.
Distinguish mint-level from account-level extensions; they live in different accounts.
For old accounts, reallocate to add the extension rather than assuming it is present.

entries.title: Account can only be closed if its withheld fee balance is zero
entries.summary: The account holds transfer fees that were withheld from past transfers. Closing it would strand them, so the program requires harvesting them to the mint first.
why: Transfers into this account withheld fees that accumulate in the account itself.
A close was attempted before the harvest instruction ran.
The fee authority never harvested, so fees piled up.
A wallet's 'close empty account' flow does not know about withheld fees.
fix: Run the harvest-to-mint instruction for this account, then close it.
Check the withheld amount first; if it is zero, the close should succeed.
If you are the fee authority, harvest periodically so accounts stay closable.
Wallets: treat a non-zero withheld balance as a pre-close step, not an error.

entries.title: Non-confidential transfers disabled
entries.summary: The mint is configured to require confidential transfers, and an ordinary transfer was attempted. Balances are encrypted on this mint, so the plain transfer path is closed.
why: The confidential-transfer extension was configured with non-confidential transfers disabled.
A wallet sent a normal transfer to a mint that only accepts confidential ones.
The mint flipped the flag after the client cached its state.
A DEX pool was created for a confidential mint that does not support plain transfers.
fix: Use a wallet that supports confidential transfers for this mint.
If you are the issuer, note that this setting makes the token unusable on standard DEXes.
Check the mint's confidential configuration before building any integration.
For plain transfers, the issuer must allow non-confidential transfers — that is their decision, not a client bug.

entries.title: Position not empty — cannot close
entries.summary: You tried to close a concentrated-liquidity position that still holds liquidity, uncollected fees, or uncollected rewards. Raydium refuses to destroy a position NFT while value is still inside it.
why: The position still has active liquidity in its price range — closing would burn tokens you own.
Fees earned from trades through your range have accumulated but were never claimed.
Reward tokens (if the pool runs an emissions program) are sitting uncollected in the position.
An integration script called close_position without running decrease_liquidity and collect_fees first.
fix: Remove all liquidity from the position first (decrease_liquidity with 100%).
Claim accumulated fees with collect_fees — do this after removing liquidity.
Claim any reward tokens with collect_reward.
Then retry close_position; it succeeds on an empty position.

entries.title: Tick out of range
entries.summary: A tick index submitted to the pool is outside the valid Raydium CLMM range of -443636 to +443636. The program bounds ticks so price math stays inside a fixed-point range.
why: A price-range request was converted to ticks incorrectly — usually a tool or script picking ticks beyond the bound.
Extreme prices (degenerate tokens, new launches) can need ticks outside the range; the pool simply cannot represent them.
A typo or sign error in a manual tick calculation.
fix: Recompute the ticks with Raydium's own tick math library and clamp to [-443636, 443636].
If your target price is genuinely beyond the bound, the position cannot be placed — pick a nearer range.
Retry from the pool UI, which always submits valid ticks.

entries.title: Tick not aligned to spacing
entries.summary: A submitted tick is not a multiple of the pool's tick_spacing. Concentrated-liquidity pools only accept price ranges on a grid — a 10-spacing pool accepts tick -120 or 130, never 127.
why: A custom range was computed from a target price without rounding to the pool's spacing.
The spacing was read from a different pool (pools with different volatility tiers use different spacings).
An integration hardcodes spacing 1 assumptions.
fix: Read tick_spacing from the pool account, then round your lower/upper ticks down/up to the nearest multiple.
Or just set the range in the UI — it snaps to the grid for you.
If copying a range from another pool, confirm both pools share the same spacing first.

entries.title: Both token amounts are zero
entries.summary: An increase-liquidity call arrived with both amount_0_max and amount_1_max set to zero. The program refuses to create an empty position.
why: A quote failed upstream and the caller passed zero amounts instead of aborting.
A bot split liquidity adds and sent one with an empty leg.
A UI state bug after a token balance reset.
fix: Retry with a real quote — at least one of the two amounts must be positive.
For one-sided ranges, the zero side is allowed, but not both zero at once.
Check token balances and approvals if your tool zeroed out amounts.

entries.title: Liquidity insufficient for withdrawal
entries.summary: A decrease-liquidity call asked for more liquidity than the position holds. This is the CLMM version of withdrawing more than you deposited.
why: The withdraw amount was computed against stale position data — liquidity can change if someone else manages the position.
A burn/fee accounting mismatch in a script that estimated liquidity from share math instead of reading the position.
A repeated withdrawal where the first one already consumed the liquidity.
fix: Re-read the position account and withdraw liquidity <= its current liquidity value.
If automating, always derive the amount from the position, never from your own ledger.
Check the position wasn't already closed or drained.

entries.title: Price slippage check
entries.summary: The swap's execution price crossed beyond the caller's slippage guard before the fill completed. Raydium CLMM's generic slippage rejection on the price itself.
why: Price moved between quote and execution — concentrated liquidity amplifies this because thin ranges move price faster.
The swap traversed far more ticks than expected, repricing each step.
The transaction landed late in congestion with a stale sqrt_price_limit.
sqrt_price_limit was set too tight (or left at a default) for the trade size.
fix: Retry with a fresh quote; most rejections clear on the next attempt.
Widen sqrt_price_limit proportionally — it is your price bound for the swap.
Add priority fee: latency is the usual culprit, not volatility.
Split large swaps into chunks so each stays inside its price bound.

entries.title: Too little output received
entries.summary: An exact-input swap produced less output than the minimum you specified (other_amount_threshold). Raydium CLMM's everyday slippage rejection — and its most common swap failure.
why: Price moved against the trade between the quote and the fill.
The swap crossed many tick boundaries, so realized output lagged the quote.
Low priority fee pushed the transaction into a later block after the price moved.
The minimum was hardcoded instead of derived from the live quote.
fix: Re-quote and resubmit — most failures clear immediately.
Widen the slippage tolerance one notch (0.5% to 1% is typical for deep pools).
Attach a priority fee so the swap lands while the quote is still valid.
For volatile new tokens, accept 2-3% or split the order.

entries.title: Too much input paid
entries.summary: An exact-output swap needed more input than the maximum you allowed (other_amount_threshold). The mirror of 6018: you fixed the output, the price moved, and the required input exceeded your cap.
why: The output target was fixed, so any adverse price move shows up as extra input required.
Liquidity thinned out in the range the swap had to traverse.
Latency: the transaction executed against a later, worse price.
max_amount_in was set from an old quote.
fix: Re-quote and raise the input cap to match, or accept a slightly smaller output.
Widen the tolerance — for exact-out swaps the cap must cover the worst realistic path.
Add priority fee to reduce time-to-land.
Consider exact-input instead: fixing the input and accepting variable output tolerates price moves better.

entries.title: Swap amount is zero
entries.summary: A swap instruction arrived with amount_specified = 0. The program treats a zero-size swap as invalid rather than a no-op.
why: The token amount was lost in a UI rounding step (0.0000004 truncated to 0).
A dust-balance swap where the wallet held effectively nothing.
An integration passed the wrong field — the amount landed in another argument.
fix: Enter an amount greater than zero, with full decimal precision.
Check the wallet actually holds a tradeable balance of the input token.
If scripting, log the instruction payload before sending to catch the mis-mapped field.

entries.title: Swap amount too small
entries.summary: The swap's input or output amount is below the smallest unit the pool's tick math can represent. Tiny trades inside a concentrated range can round to zero liquidity movement and are rejected outright.
why: A micro trade (fractions of a cent) rounds to nothing in the fixed-point math.
A token with very few decimals makes even normal-sized trades round small.
A retry loop kept resubmitting a shrinking dust amount after earlier failures.
fix: Increase the trade size above the pool's minimum representable amount.
For low-decimal tokens, compute the minimum viable amount from the mint's decimals.
Stop retry chains once amounts fall below the dust threshold — the error will repeat forever.

entries.title: Not enough tick array accounts
entries.summary: The swap's remaining_accounts carried fewer tick-array accounts than the trade needs to traverse its price path. Concentrated-liquidity swaps must pass the tick arrays covering every step of the route.
why: The trade was larger than the arrays provided — it needs to sweep more price space than the caller anticipated.
The start tick array was computed from a stale pool price, so the array list missed where the price actually sits.
An integration only ever passes one array while big swaps need several.
fix: Re-derive the tick array sequence from the current pool price before building the swap.
Split the swap so each leg fits inside the arrays already provided.
Use the SDK's swap builder, which assembles the correct array list automatically.

entries.title: Token-2022 extension not supported
entries.summary: The pool does not support the Token-2022 mint extensions this token uses. Raydium CLMM only enables specific extensions (like transfer fee) per pool; a token carrying unsupported extensions cannot be swapped in it.
why: The token is a Token-2022 mint with extensions the pool was not initialized to accept.
The pool supports transfer-fee tokens but this mint uses, say, transfer hooks or confidential transfers.
A mint was swapped into a legacy SPL-Token pool by mistake.
fix: Swap this token in a pool explicitly initialized for its extension set, or route via an aggregator that finds one.
If you create pools, initialize with the right extension flags for the mints involved.
Check the mint's extensions on an explorer before wiring it into CLMM pools.

entries.title: Not enough liquidity in this direction
entries.summary: The pool has no (or too little) liquidity on the side of the price your swap direction needs. Concentrated liquidity is directional: if all LP ranges sit above the current price, sells into the low side simply have nothing to trade against.
why: All active ranges were withdrawn — LPs pulled liquidity, leaving one side empty.
Price drifted to the edge of every range, exhausting one side's liquidity.
A very thin new pool where one direction barely has deposits.
Trading a token whose owners market-sold the entire bid-side range.
fix: Check the pool's current liquidity distribution before trading; if one side is empty, the swap cannot fill.
Route through an aggregator that splits across pools with liquidity on the needed side.
Wait for LPs to redeposit, or trade a different pair with deeper ranges.

entries.title: Transfer fee calculation mismatch
entries.summary: The pool's internal transfer-fee arithmetic disagreed with the token's actual Token-2022 transfer fee config. This surfaces when a transfer-fee token's fee rate changed after the pool was created.
why: The token's transfer fee was updated (epoch-based fee changes) and the pool's expectations went stale.
A CPI charged a different fee than the pool pre-computed for the vault transfer.
The pool was initialized against a different epoch's fee schedule.
fix: Retry after the epoch boundary if the fee just changed — state refresh often clears it.
Route around pools holding this token until the pool operator re-initializes for the new fee.
For token issuers: don't rotate transfer-fee rates on mints that live in CLMM pools without coordinating.

entries.title: Fee calculation failure
entries.summary: The pool's fee arithmetic failed mid-swap — the dynamic fee (base fee plus volatility-based adjustments) produced a value the math could not apply.
why: The pool's volatility accumulator produced a dynamic fee outside the computable range.
A malformed fee curve configuration for this pool type.
Extremely large trade sizes pushing the fee multiplication into overflow.
fix: Retry — transient accumulator states usually resolve on the next attempt.
Split the trade into smaller chunks if the size is extreme.
Route via an aggregator to a different pool if it repeats on this one.

entries.title: Exceeded slippage tolerance
entries.summary: The swap's realized price moved past the caller's slippage tolerance. The standard slippage rejection on Meteora's classic AMM pools — its most common swap failure.
why: Price moved between the quote and execution.
The pool is thin, so even a modest trade reprices it past the tolerance.
The transaction landed late under congestion.
The tolerance was copied from a different, deeper pool's settings.
fix: Re-quote and resubmit — most clear on the next attempt.
Widen slippage one step (0.5% to 1%); for thin pools 2-3%.
Add a priority fee so the swap lands while the quote is fresh.
Split large trades; each chunk re-quotes against the live pool state.

entries.title: Zero trading tokens
entries.summary: The requested pool-token amount results in zero underlying trading tokens — a deposit or withdrawal so small that after invariants it maps to nothing on at least one side of the pool.
why: A dust LP deposit where one side's token amount rounds to zero.
A withdrawal computed from a stale LP balance.
A pool heavily imbalanced in a way that makes small two-sided deposits impossible.
fix: Increase the deposit size so both sides receive a non-zero amount.
For withdrawals, redeem a larger LP share or check the LP balance is current.
Check the pool's reserves — if one side is near-empty, two-sided ops may be impossible at small sizes.

entries.title: Pool disabled
entries.summary: The pool's enabled flag is off — swaps are administratively paused. Nothing in your transaction is wrong; the pool itself is closed for trading.
why: The pool operator disabled trading (maintenance, migration, or incident response).
A deprecated pool left disabled after liquidity moved to a new program version.
An exploit response froze the pool temporarily.
fix: Wait for the operator to re-enable; there is no user-side workaround on this pool.
Route to a different pool for the same pair — aggregators do this automatically when you refresh the quote.
Check Meteora's announcements if the outage is broad.

entries.title: Source and destination are the same
entries.summary: The swap's source and destination token accounts are the same account. Swapping a token to itself is rejected as meaningless.
why: The input and output mints resolved to the same token (a route-building bug).
An ATA was passed for both legs by mistake.
A wrapped/native SOL handling error made both sides the same account.
fix: Rebuild the route so input and output are genuinely different tokens.
Check the route plan if you swap via an aggregator — a degenerate hop can appear in custom routes.
Verify the destination ATA belongs to the output mint.

entries.title: Depeg mint mismatch
entries.summary: Token mint B does not match the depeg-type pool's configured pegged mint. Depeg pools track stablecoin pegs explicitly; the token passed is not the one the pool was built for.
why: A stable of the same family (but different issuer) was passed to a pool configured for another one.
The pool's depeg info references an older mint after the stable migrated.
A route builder matched pools by symbol instead of mint address.
fix: Use the exact mint address the pool config specifies — match by address, never by symbol.
Refresh pool config; if the stable re-issued its mint, the pool must be updated on the protocol side.
Route to a generic (non-depeg) pool for odd stable pairs.

entries.title: Token amount is not 1:1
entries.summary: A depeg-pool operation expected a 1:1 token amount but received something else. These pools assume the stable trades at par; amounts that imply a depeg are rejected in the admin/rebalance paths.
why: The stable actually depegged and pool math saw a non-par ratio.
A rebalance/deposit path passed amounts computed from a par assumption while the market no longer trades at par.
A transfer-fee ate part of the amount, breaking the expected 1:1.
fix: Check the stable's market price — if it has depegged, this pool's guarantees are off.
Recompute amounts including any transfer fee on the token.
Trade through a non-depeg pool while the peg is disturbed.

entries.title: Amount is zero
entries.summary: A pool operation arrived with a zero amount. Swaps, deposits and withdrawals all require a non-zero size.
why: A UI rounding step truncated a dust amount to zero.
An integration passed the wrong field into the instruction.
A retry loop shrank the amount to nothing after repeated failures.
fix: Enter a real amount with full decimal precision.
Verify the wallet holds a balance worth trading.
In scripts, validate the amount is non-zero before building the instruction.

entries.title: Amount is not enough
entries.summary: The provided amount is below what the operation requires — typically a withdrawal or burn asking for more value than the account actually holds, or a swap input short of the pool's effective minimum.
why: The user's token balance is smaller than the requested size (stale balance display).
An LP withdrawal exceeded the wallet's actual LP token holdings.
The pool enforces a minimum operation size and the request sits below it.
fix: Refresh balances and request an amount <= what you actually hold.
Round withdrawals slightly under the LP balance to absorb rounding.
Check the pool's minimum swap/deposit size if the balance looks sufficient.

entries.title: Pool is not a launch pool
entries.summary: A launch-specific operation (activation-point configuration, launch-phase behavior) was invoked on an ordinary pool. Meteora's launch pools carry extra state that normal pools don't have.
why: A bot targeted the wrong pool of the same pair (launch variant vs regular variant).
The token graduated from its launch pool and further launch ops are invalid.
A script reused launch-pool instruction builders for every pool.
fix: Confirm which pool variant you are targeting before sending launch-specific instructions.
After graduation, use normal swap/deposit paths — launch ops no longer apply.
If automating, branch on the pool's config type instead of assuming launch.

entries.title: Activation point cannot be modified
entries.summary: An attempt to change the pool's activation point was rejected. The activation point — the moment trading goes live on a launch pool — is fixed once set (or once trading is imminent) so participants cannot be rug-moved in time.
why: The modification window has closed — the point locks as launch approaches.
The caller is not the pool authority.
The pool has already activated; activation points are history at that stage.
fix: Nothing to fix as a trader — if a launch you follow moves its start time, treat that as a red flag, not a bug.
For pool operators: schedule the activation point correctly at creation; it will not be editable later.

entries.title: Invalid activation point
entries.summary: The activation point supplied at pool creation is invalid — out of the allowed time window or in the wrong format for the chosen activation type.
why: The timestamp is in the past or beyond the allowed maximum lead time.
The activation point conflicts with the pool's activation type (slot-based vs timestamp).
A malformed number was passed in a pool-creation script.
fix: Create the pool with a future activation point inside the protocol's allowed window.
Match the point's semantics to the activation type (slot number vs unix timestamp).
Traders: an invalid activation on a new launch just means the launch was misconfigured — expect it to be redeployed.

entries.title: Swap attempted before activation
entries.summary: A swap hit a launch pool during its pre-activation window. Trading is intentionally locked until the activation point passes — sniping attempts inside the window are rejected by design.
why: You tried to buy a newly launched token before its activation point.
A bot fired at its scheduled time but the transaction landed in the pre-activation window.
Clock skew: your client's clock disagrees with Solana's slot/timestamp reality.
fix: Wait until the activation point passes, then swap normally — this error is the guard working.
If automating, target the first slot after activation, not the activation slot itself.
Do not pay escalating priority fees to force it; the rejection is deterministic until activation.

entries.title: Quote token must be SOL or USDC
entries.summary: A pool creation attempted to use a quote mint other than SOL or USDC. Meteora launch pools standardize on these two quote tokens; anything else is rejected at creation.
why: A token deployer tried to configure an exotic quote token for a launch pool.
A script mixed up base and quote mints.
A wrapped variant of SOL/USDC was passed instead of the canonical mints.
fix: Create launch pools with canonical SOL or USDC as the quote mint.
Traders: a failed creation means the launch was misconfigured — the token will likely redeploy.
Check you're using the native SOL mint (or native USDC), not a wrapped derivative.

entries.title: Input does not match curve config
entries.summary: The buy or sell parameters don't match the pool's curve type. LaunchLab pools run configurable bonding curves, and every trade must use the quote math of the curve the pool was created with.
why: A bot assumed the default linear curve while the pool was created with a different curve type.
The SDK version used to build the instruction is older than the curve config on-chain.
Manual instruction construction passed wrong flags for the curve variant.
fix: Read the pool's curve config and use the matching quote function from the current SDK.
Update the client SDK — curve variants were added over time and old builders hardcode the first one.
For manual trades, switch to the pool's official UI; it always builds the right instruction.

entries.title: Exceeded slippage tolerance
entries.summary: A launch-pad buy or sell moved past the slippage limit you allowed. On a fresh LaunchLab pool price discovery is violent, so this is the single most common failure for early buyers.
why: Price on the bonding curve moved between quote and execution — early pools move on every trade.
Someone else's buy landed first and shifted the curve against you.
The transaction was delayed by congestion while the curve kept moving.
Slippage was set to the tight default from a mature-pool mindset.
fix: Re-quote and retry; on launch curves expect to retry several times.
Widen slippage for the first minutes after launch — 5-15% is normal on brand-new pools, then tighten as the curve deepens.
Add priority fee so the transaction lands in the same slot as the quote.
Watch the pool's trade feed before entering: if buys are landing every slot, your quote is stale before it arrives.

entries.title: Pool is still in funding
entries.summary: The pool has not finished its funding phase, so the operation is not available yet. LaunchLab pools can raise before trading opens; until funding completes, trades are rejected.
why: You tried to buy during the pre-trading funding window.
A bot fired at pool-creation time instead of at the trading-open time.
The pool's funding target has not been reached yet.
fix: Wait for the funding phase to complete — the pool's state flips when the target fills.
If automating, watch the pool account's status field rather than a fixed timer.
Check the launch page for the announced trading-open time.

entries.title: Pool already migrated
entries.summary: The token has graduated: its LaunchLab pool migrated to a standard Raydium pool, and the old bonding-curve pool no longer trades. This is the LaunchLab equivalent of pump.fun's 6081.
why: The curve completed and liquidity moved to a CPMM pool.
A saved link or bot config still targets the graduated pool address.
You bought from a stale quote built before migration.
fix: Find the new CPMM pool for the token and trade there — the launch page links it after graduation.
Refresh your bot's pool address; migrated pools are permanently closed.
If a UI still shows the launch pool, clear cache or use Raydium's main swap page.

entries.title: Migration type mismatch
entries.summary: A migration call named a migration target type the pool wasn't configured for. LaunchLab pools declare where they graduate to at creation; the migrate instruction must match it.
why: An integration assumed the default migration target (CPMM) while the pool was configured for another.
Manual migration with the wrong type flag.
A pool created with a non-standard config being migrated by a generic script.
fix: Read the pool's migration config and pass the matching type.
Use the official migration path (UI or current SDK) — it reads the config for you.
Traders hitting this indirectly: the migration simply hasn't happened yet; the launch page will show the new pool when it does.

entries.title: Nothing to collect
entries.summary: A creator fee-claim or vesting-collect call found no assets to collect. Either fees haven't accrued yet, or they were already claimed in an earlier transaction.
why: No trading fees have accrued since the last claim.
A duplicate claim in the same block — the first one emptied the balance.
The pool has had no volume since launch.
fix: Wait for trading volume, then claim again.
Check the claim history before retrying — double-claims always return this.
If you're a creator with a vesting schedule, confirm it has started (6012 is the error when it hasn't).

entries.title: Vesting has not started
entries.summary: A vesting claim was attempted before the schedule's start time. Creator allocations on LaunchLab unlock on a timer; claiming early is rejected by design.
why: The vesting cliff hasn't been reached yet.
The schedule's start time is after the current block timestamp.
A script computed the start time from local clock instead of on-chain state.
fix: Wait until the vesting start time passes.
Read the vesting schedule account for the exact unlock timestamp instead of guessing.
For token buyers: early creator claims failing is expected and healthy — allocation is locked.

entries.title: No vesting schedule
entries.summary: A vesting claim was attempted on a pool that has no vesting schedule at all. The creator chose full unlock at launch, so there is nothing to vest.
why: The pool was created without a vesting configuration.
The vesting account passed belongs to a different pool.
A generic creator tool always attempts vesting claims regardless of config.
fix: Nothing to claim — if the creator has no vesting, allocation was fully liquid from day one.
Verify you're using the right pool's vesting account.
Traders: absence of vesting is a token-quality signal worth noting, not an error to fix.

entries.title: Pool not migrated yet
entries.summary: An operation that requires a graduated pool was called while the pool is still on the bonding curve. Post-migration actions — like trading on the CPMM side — are unavailable until graduation happens.
why: You tried to interact with the post-migration pool before the curve completed.
A bot pre-built the CPMM trade for a token that hasn't graduated.
The token is close to graduation and someone front-ran the migration.
fix: Trade on the launch pool while it's still on the curve; it works until the moment of migration.
If automating, branch on pool status: curve phase → launch instructions, migrated → CPMM instructions.
Wait for graduation if your strategy requires the CPMM pool specifically.

entries.title: Token-2022 extension not supported
entries.summary: The token uses a Token-2022 extension LaunchLab pools don't accept. LaunchLab supports only a specific extension set (transfer fee among them); others block pool creation and trading.
why: The mint carries an unsupported extension such as transfer hooks or confidential transfers.
A creator launched with an extension set that predates LaunchLab support.
The wrong mint was wired into a trading script.
fix: Use a mint without unsupported extensions for launch pools.
Traders: if a token's pool fails this way, the launch is broken — expect a redeploy with a clean mint.
Check extensions on an explorer before building tools around a mint.

entries.title: Not enough remaining accounts
entries.summary: The instruction was sent without all the remaining accounts the curve math needs. LaunchLab trades reference multiple curve-state accounts, and a missing one aborts the transaction.
why: A hand-built transaction omitted one of the required curve accounts.
The pool type changed (for example after a curve update) and the account list is now longer.
An SDK version mismatch produced an outdated account list.
fix: Rebuild the transaction with the current SDK, which fetches the full account list.
For manual builds, compare your account list against the IDL's accounts for that instruction.
Update the client; account requirements are versioned with the program.

entries.title: Transfer fee calculation mismatch
entries.summary: The LaunchLab pool's transfer-fee arithmetic disagreed with the token's Token-2022 fee config. Surfaces when a transfer-fee token changes its rate after the pool was created.
why: The token's transfer fee was updated (epoch-based changes) after pool creation.
A CPI charged a fee different from the pool's precomputed expectation.
Pool initialized against an older fee schedule.
fix: Retry after the epoch boundary if the fee just changed.
Route around the pool until the operator refreshes its fee state.
Creators: don't rotate transfer-fee rates on launched mints without coordinating.

entries.title: Limit order already filled
entries.summary: A modify or cancel call targeted a limit order that is already fully filled. Once filled, an order is final — there is nothing left to change.
why: Price crossed your limit while the transaction was in flight.
A cancel was sent after the keeper bot had already executed the order.
A batch script retried a modify on an order filled by the first attempt.
fix: Read the order account before modifying — filled orders are immutable.
Treat the fill as done: your tokens were swapped at your limit price.
In automations, check order status in the same transaction context as the modify.

entries.title: Invalid limit order phase
entries.summary: The requested operation doesn't apply to the order's current phase. Limit orders move through phases (open, partially filled, filled, expired) and each phase permits only certain actions.
why: A modify was attempted on an order that already expired.
A cancel targeted an order in a closed phase.
Manual order management used the wrong phase assumption.
fix: Read the order's phase state before acting; match the operation to the phase.
For expired orders, no action is needed — the escrowed funds are released by the protocol's expiry path.
Use the official UI for one-off management; it only offers valid actions per phase.

entries.title: Invalid limit order amount
entries.summary: A limit order was created or modified with an amount the pool can't represent — zero, below the minimum order size, or beyond a tick-range bound.
why: The order amount rounds to zero in the pool's fixed-point math.
The amount is below the protocol's minimum order size.
A modify tried to grow the order beyond the escrowed balance.
fix: Enter an amount above the pool's minimum order size.
Fund the escrow for the full order amount before creating it.
For low-decimal tokens, compute the minimum in base units rather than UI units.

entries.title: Invalid activation duration
entries.summary: The launch pool's activation window was configured with an out-of-range duration. The protocol caps how long after activation a launch pool can keep its special launch parameters.
why: Pool creation passed a duration beyond the allowed maximum.
A zero or negative duration (malformed number) was supplied.
A script used a different program version's limit.
fix: Create the pool with a duration inside the protocol's allowed range.
Traders: a failed creation means the launch needs redeploying — the pool you see won't trade.
Pull limits from the current program constants rather than hardcoding.

entries.title: Invalid activation type
entries.summary: The pool was created with an unrecognized activation type. Launch pools activate by slot or by timestamp; anything else is rejected.
why: A value outside the enum (slot / timestamp) was passed at creation.
A serialized config from another program was reused.
Client and program versions disagree on the enum.
fix: Use a supported activation type when creating a pool.
Update the client SDK so the enum matches the program.
Traders: an invalid activation type means a failed deploy, not a trading bug.

entries.title: Invalid pool type
entries.summary: An instruction doesn't apply to this pool's type. Meteora AMM pools come in variants (standard, stable/depeg, launch) and type-specific instructions are rejected on the wrong variant.
why: A launch-only instruction was sent to a standard pool.
A depeg-specific call hit a constant-product pool.
A generic bot assumed one pool layout for all variants.
fix: Read the pool's type flag first and branch your instruction set accordingly.
Use the official SDK, which dispatches per pool type.
If you only need a swap, the swap instruction works across variants — stay on the generic path.

entries.title: Incorrect associated token account
entries.summary: One of the token accounts passed is not the canonical associated token account (ATA) for the expected mint and owner. Meteora validates ATAs explicitly in its zap and LP paths.
why: A non-canonical token account (created manually) was used where an ATA is required.
The ATA of a different mint or owner was passed.
The ATA was never created, so a placeholder address was sent.
fix: Derive the ATA with the standard associated-token-account program and create it first if missing.
Use wallet defaults: most wallets pass the canonical ATA automatically.
For scripts, assert the account equals getAssociatedTokenAddress(mint, owner) before sending.

entries.title: Invalid zap accounts
entries.summary: A zap in/out (one-click LP add or remove) was sent with an account list that doesn't match what the zap path expects — typically a missing intermediate token account or a wrong pool vault.
why: A custom zap implementation omitted one of the required intermediate accounts.
The zap route swapped through a token pair the pool doesn't pair with.
Accounts were assembled from stale pool data.
fix: Use the official zap SDK entry point — it assembles the full account list.
Fall back to plain deposit/withdraw plus a separate swap if you control the transaction.
Re-fetch pool state right before building the zap.

entries.title: Not the owner of the LP token account
entries.summary: The signer does not own the LP token account being redeemed. Withdrawals must be signed by the authority of the LP account holding the pool shares.
why: The connected wallet differs from the one that deposited.
An LP token account was passed that belongs to another wallet.
Delegated or shared-wallet setups where the signer isn't the LP account owner.
fix: Withdraw from the wallet that holds the LP tokens.
Switch accounts in the wallet if you deposited from a different one.
For custodial setups, the account owner (or its delegate) must sign.
